# Partnerships to Achieve Student Success National Cohorts

*   [Blog](https://www.thirdsectorcap.org/types/blog/)

### Partnerships to Achieve Student Success National Cohorts Third Sector is Supporting States to Direct Public Dollars Toward Evidence-Based Support Services that Address Barriers to Postsecondary Education

[Dr. Joy Coates](https://www.thirdsectorcap.org/author/jcoates/)August 28, 2024

*   [](http://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https://www.thirdsectorcap.org/blog/partnerships-to-achieve-student-success-national-cohorts/&t=Partnerships%20to%20Achieve%20Student%20Success%20National%20Cohorts)
*   [](http://twitter.com/home?status=Partnerships%20to%20Achieve%20Student%20Success%20National%20Cohorts%20https://www.thirdsectorcap.org/blog/partnerships-to-achieve-student-success-national-cohorts/)
*   [](http://linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https://www.thirdsectorcap.org/blog/partnerships-to-achieve-student-success-national-cohorts/&title=Partnerships%20to%20Achieve%20Student%20Success%20National%20Cohorts)
*   [](mailto:?subject=Partnerships%20to%20Achieve%20Student%20Success%20National%20Cohorts&body=https://www.thirdsectorcap.org/blog/partnerships-to-achieve-student-success-national-cohorts/)

# The Opportunity

Everyone, no matter their age, race, zip code, or previous educational background deserves to get the education and the career they want. And yet millions of Americans face significant barriers to enrolling, persisting, and completing postsecondary education and obtaining a credential – even as[more and more of the best paying jobs require some kind of postsecondary education](https://www.thirdway.org/report/ripple-effect-the-cost-of-the-college-dropout-rate).

At the same time, there are a variety of wraparound student support services and promising practices offered by providers across the country that have demonstrated success in improving outcomes for students who face more barriers to college than others by meeting their specific needs and removing those barriers. While the evidence for these services, programs, and policies continues to grow, many states are not investing at the level necessary to achieve impact.

The Partnerships to Achieve Student Success (PASS) cohort envisions a future in which public systems of higher education strategically invest in the resources, evidence-informed wraparound support services, and policies necessary to support college-seeking students who face the most significant barriers to enrollment, persistence, and graduation.

# The Cohorts

Third Sector provided the cohorts with six months of technical assistance, cross-cohort peer learning, and field-building to:

*   Identify disparities in outcomes using disaggregated data sets;
*   Refine the challenge they are seeking to address by learning more about the population most impacted by barriers to higher education in their states and critically examine root causes of the challenge; and
*   Engage stakeholders in the co-design of solution(s) to address the challenge.

By the end of each cohort, states co-created implementation plans with Third Sector that outlined the data-informed challenge they are seeking to address, the specific subpopulation of students most impacted, root causes of the challenge and corresponding population needs, a solution co-designed with stakeholders, and clear next steps for how they might leverage policies, support services, data, and funding to implement the solution.

Zoom level changed to 1

### 2019

In 2019, Third Sector formed the first Partnerships to Achieve Student Success (PASS) cohort, with support from the Kresge Foundation, to create partnerships with state systems of higher education across the country to engage in innovative, outcomes-driven approaches to supporting students with historically low enrollment, persistence, and completion rates. Third Sector worked with Arizona (Arizona State University), Colorado (Colorado Department of Higher Education), Connecticut (Connecticut State Colleges & Universities), and Ohio (Ohio Department of Higher Education) to innovate new outcomes-based approaches to identifying and supporting various groups of students with historically low completion rates in getting to and through college. As a result of the cohort, the Colorado Department of Higher Education’s Colorado Opportunity Scholarship Initiative launched the Finish What You Started Adams County pilot, which provides social, financial, and career supports to help adult learners 25 and older with some college, no degree – particularly those identifying as Black/African American, Hispanic/Latino/a, and Native American – return to higher education and complete a degree or certificate. Third Sector continues to work with the Ohio Department of Higher Education, with support from the Kresge and ECMC Foundations, to pilot similar investments in wraparound student supports for Ohio National Guard members.

[Ohio Coach to Complete](https://www.thirdsectorcap.org/)

Third Sector continued to work with the Ohio Department of Higher Education, with support from the Kresge and ECMC Foundations, to pilot investments in coaching services provided by InsideTrack for first-year [Ohio National Guard](https://www.thirdsectorcap.org/news/cuyahoga-national-guard-pfs-contract/)scholarship recipients in Cuyahoga County, using a Pay for Success (PFS) or social impact bond (SIB) financing model. The program, “Coach to Complete,” will serve up to 510 eligible Ohio guardsmen from Northeast Ohio, in partnership with the Cuyahoga County Department of Health and Human Services.

*   September 2023: [“Cuyahoga County Launches New Success Coaching Program to Help National Guard Members Access and Complete Higher Education”](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/cuyahoga-county-launches-new-success-coaching-program-to-help-national-guard-members-access-and-complete-higher-education-301931695.html)

[Colorado Finish What You Started](https://www.thirdsectorcap.org/)

Third Sector continued to work with the Colorado Opportunity Scholarship Initiative (COSI) through the pandemic and successfully launched the [Finish What You Started pilot in Adams County, Colorado](https://www.thirdsectorcap.org/news/colorado-opportunity-scholarship-initiative-and-one-million-degrees-launch-finish-what-you-started/), which provides social, financial, and career supports to adults with some college, no degree – particularly those identifying as Black/African American, Hispanic/Latino/a, and Native American – to return to higher education and complete a degree or certificate using an innovative, equity-centered outcomes-based contract with service provider One Million Degrees. Finish What You Started is among the first outcomes-based contracts for support services in the field of higher education nationwide. With the passage of H.B. 21-1330, signed by Governor Polis on June 29, 2021, COSI received $48 million of American Rescue Plan (ARP) funding to expand Finish What You Started statewide, allocating funding to all Colorado public institutions of higher education to provide direct and indirect support to students and expanding the population eligible to participate.

*   August 2020: [Colorado and Ohio Leading the Nation in Collaborative and Innovative Pay for Success Projects in Higher Education](https://www.thirdsectorcap.org/news/colorado-and-ohio-leading-the-nation-in-collaborative-and-innovative-pay-for-success-projects-in-higher-education/)
*   April 2021: [Colorado Opportunity Scholarship Initiative and One Million Degrees launch “Finish What You Started”](https://www.thirdsectorcap.org/news/colorado-opportunity-scholarship-initiative-and-one-million-degrees-launch-finish-what-you-started/)
*   April 2023: [Hundreds of thousands of Coloradans have some college credits. This program gives them a second chance at a degree](https://coloradosun.com/2023/04/20/colorado-college-degree-partial-credit-higher-education/)

### 2022

In the second PASS cohort, launched in 2022 with support from the ECMC Foundation, Third Sector partnered with the Alabama (Alabama Commission on Higher Education), Michigan (Michigan Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity (LEO) Office of Sixty by 30), and Rhode Island (Rhode Island Office of the Postsecondary Commissioner) – all of whom were interested in better-serving adults with some college, no degree. Through the 2022 PASS Cohort, partners developed a deep understanding of adults 25 and older with some college experience, but no degree in their state and designing customized solutions that improve their ability to more effectively serve all returning adults, no matter what led to breaks in their education, and eliminate equity gaps between different groups of adults. Recognizing that adults have unique needs and challenges that prevent them from enrolling in and completing college, we support our PASS Cohort partners in taking a population-first approach, designing strategies that enable them to develop a deeper understanding of lived experiences for individuals in this population as well as examine root and systemic causes of lower degree attainment. Following the second PASS Cohort, Third Sector continued to support Alabama (Alabama Commission on Higher Education) on the implementation of their action plan.

[(Re)Engage Alabama](https://www.thirdsectorcap.org/)

Third Sector continued to work with Alabama t o advance their state’s commitment to supporting adult learners. [ACHE](http://ache.edu/), [Alabama Possible](https://alabamapossible.org/), and the [Governor's Office of Education and Workforce Transformation](https://governor.alabama.gov/assets/2019/09/Governor-Ivey-GOEWT-Office-Internship.pdf) launched [(Re)Engage Alabama](https://alabamapossible.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/ReEngage-Alabama-Executive-Summary.pdf), an adult attainment-focused learning community, in partnership with Third Sector. Between August 2022 and August 2023, ACHE and Alabama Possible hosted five convenings, co-facilitated by Third Sector and with support from Education Strategy Group (ESG), to elevate best practices from the field, share statewide and institutional adult student outcomes data, and enable cross-institution relationship building and problem-solving. This effort also played a role in passing S.B. 175 establishing the ReEngage Alabama Grant Program, $4.5M in scholarships for returning adult students pursuing in-demand credentials.

### 2024

In May 2024, Third Sector launched the Partnerships to Achieve Student Success (PASS) 3 cohort to create cross-sector partnerships with community-based organizations, workforce organizations, state systems of higher education, and other key stakeholders to explore ways states can apply innovative, outcomes-driven approaches to scale or strengthen initiatives that re-engage adult learners in earning a credential and/or connecting them to better jobs.

Third Sector will leverage its expertise in outcomes-based approaches, continuous improvement, stakeholder engagement, and partnership development to support coordinated state-level strategy-building pathways that engage adult learners and connect them to better jobs. The state partners in this cohort are Indiana and Mississippi.[Learn more here](https://www.thirdsectorcap.org/portfolio/partnerships-to-achieve-student-success-national-cohort/).

# The Opportunity

Everyone, no matter their age, race, zip code, or previous educational background deserves to get the education and the career they want. And yet millions of Americans face significant barriers to enrolling, persisting, and completing postsecondary education and obtaining a credential – even as[more and more of the best paying jobs require some kind of postsecondary education](https://www.thirdway.org/report/ripple-effect-the-cost-of-the-college-dropout-rate).

At the same time, there are a variety of wraparound student support services and promising practices offered by providers across the country that have demonstrated success in improving outcomes for students who face more barriers to college than others by meeting their specific needs and removing those barriers. While the evidence for these services, programs, and policies continues to grow, many states are not investing at the level necessary to achieve impact.

The Partnerships to Achieve Student Success (PASS) cohort envisions a future in which public systems of higher education strategically invest in the resources, evidence-informed wraparound support services, and policies necessary to support college-seeking students who face the most significant barriers to enrollment, persistence, and graduation.

# The Cohorts

Third Sector provided the cohorts with six months of technical assistance, cross-cohort peer learning, and field-building to:

*   Identify disparities in outcomes using disaggregated data sets;
*   Refine the challenge they are seeking to address by learning more about the population most impacted by barriers to higher education in their states and critically examine root causes of the challenge; and
*   Engage stakeholders in the co-design of solution(s) to address the challenge.

By the end of each cohort, states co-created implementation plans with Third Sector that outlined the data-informed challenge they are seeking to address, the specific subpopulation of students most impacted, root causes of the challenge and corresponding population needs, a solution co-designed with stakeholders, and clear next steps for how they might leverage policies, support services, data, and funding to implement the solution.

### 2019

In 2019, Third Sector formed the first Partnerships to Achieve Student Success (PASS) cohort, with support from the Kresge Foundation, to create partnerships with state systems of higher education across the country to engage in innovative, outcomes-driven approaches to supporting students with historically low enrollment, persistence, and completion rates. Third Sector worked with Arizona (Arizona State University), Colorado (Colorado Department of Higher Education), Connecticut (Connecticut State Colleges & Universities), and Ohio (Ohio Department of Higher Education) to innovate new outcomes-based approaches to identifying and supporting various groups of students with historically low completion rates in getting to and through college. As a result of the cohort, the Colorado Department of Higher Education’s Colorado Opportunity Scholarship Initiative launched the Finish What You Started Adams County pilot, which provides social, financial, and career supports to help adult learners 25 and older with some college, no degree – particularly those identifying as Black/African American, Hispanic/Latino/a, and Native American – return to higher education and complete a degree or certificate. Third Sector continues to work with the Ohio Department of Higher Education, with support from the Kresge and ECMC Foundations, to pilot similar investments in wraparound student supports for Ohio National Guard members.

[Ohio Coach to Complete](https://www.thirdsectorcap.org/)

Third Sector continued to work with the Ohio Department of Higher Education, with support from the Kresge and ECMC Foundations, to pilot investments in coaching services provided by InsideTrack for first-year [Ohio National Guard](https://www.thirdsectorcap.org/news/cuyahoga-national-guard-pfs-contract/)scholarship recipients in Cuyahoga County, using a Pay for Success (PFS) or social impact bond (SIB) financing model. The program, “Coach to Complete,” will serve up to 510 eligible Ohio guardsmen from Northeast Ohio, in partnership with the Cuyahoga County Department of Health and Human Services.

*   September 2023: [“Cuyahoga County Launches New Success Coaching Program to Help National Guard Members Access and Complete Higher Education”](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/cuyahoga-county-launches-new-success-coaching-program-to-help-national-guard-members-access-and-complete-higher-education-301931695.html)

[Colorado Finish What You Started](https://www.thirdsectorcap.org/)

Third Sector continued to work with the Colorado Opportunity Scholarship Initiative (COSI) through the pandemic and successfully launched the [Finish What You Started pilot in Adams County, Colorado](https://www.thirdsectorcap.org/news/colorado-opportunity-scholarship-initiative-and-one-million-degrees-launch-finish-what-you-started/), which provides social, financial, and career supports to adults with some college, no degree – particularly those identifying as Black/African American, Hispanic/Latino/a, and Native American – to return to higher education and complete a degree or certificate using an innovative, equity-centered outcomes-based contract with service provider One Million Degrees. Finish What You Started is among the first outcomes-based contracts for support services in the field of higher education nationwide. With the passage of H.B. 21-1330, signed by Governor Polis on June 29, 2021, COSI received $48 million of American Rescue Plan (ARP) funding to expand Finish What You Started statewide, allocating funding to all Colorado public institutions of higher education to provide direct and indirect support to students and expanding the population eligible to participate.

*   August 2020: [Colorado and Ohio Leading the Nation in Collaborative and Innovative Pay for Success Projects in Higher Education](https://www.thirdsectorcap.org/news/colorado-and-ohio-leading-the-nation-in-collaborative-and-innovative-pay-for-success-projects-in-higher-education/)
*   April 2021: [Colorado Opportunity Scholarship Initiative and One Million Degrees launch “Finish What You Started”](https://www.thirdsectorcap.org/news/colorado-opportunity-scholarship-initiative-and-one-million-degrees-launch-finish-what-you-started/)

### 2022

In the second PASS cohort, launched in 2022 with support from the ECMC Foundation, Third Sector partnered with the Alabama (Alabama Commission on Higher Education), Michigan (Michigan Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity (LEO) Office of Sixty by 30), and Rhode Island (Rhode Island Office of the Postsecondary Commissioner) – all of whom were interested in better-serving adults with some college, no degree. Through the 2022 PASS Cohort, partners developed a deep understanding of adults 25 and older with some college experience, but no degree in their state and designing customized solutions that improve their ability to more effectively serve all returning adults, no matter what led to breaks in their education, and eliminate equity gaps between different groups of adults. Recognizing that adults have unique needs and challenges that prevent them from enrolling in and completing college, we support our PASS Cohort partners in taking a population-first approach, designing strategies that enable them to develop a deeper understanding of lived experiences for individuals in this population as well as examine root and systemic causes of lower degree attainment. Following the second PASS Cohort, Third Sector continued to support Alabama (Alabama Commission on Higher Education) on the implementation of their action plan.

# Believing and Achieving: Gendered Pathways Toward Upward Educational Mobility in the United States

[Mark W. Lee](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=%22Lee%20M%22[Author])

### Mark W. Lee

PMCID: PMC7968472 PMID: [32506352](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32506352/)

## Abstract

Little research has investigated the impact of adolescent motivational resources, other than educational plans, on adult educational attainment, or whether their effects differ by gender and social class. Data from the St. Paul Youth Development Study (n=874, 55% female, 30% children of college graduates) are used to estimate a second-order latent motivation factor encompassing adolescent (age 15–16) educational plans, academic self-concept, economic self-efficacy, and mastery. Then, using logistic regression, the effect of this second-order factor on odds of college graduation in adulthood (ages 26–27 to 37–38) is estimated. Heterogenous effects of motivation by gender and parental education are investigated. The results show that the second-order motivation factor had strong positive effects on educational attainment after adjusting for family background variables. The effect of motivation did not differ by gender in the whole sample nor among children of college graduates. However, among children of less-educated parents, women were found to benefit more than men from these psychological assets for achieving upward educational mobility. These findings suggest that adolescent motivation, especially among U.S. women whose parents do not have college degrees, may be a resource for higher educational attainment.

**Keywords:**agency, intergenerational mobility, education, gender

## Introduction

Social and developmental psychologists, as well as life course sociologists, argue that inequality is a multi-level phenomenon involving influences from the genetic to the political spheres. Having the potential to enhance purposeful action within structurally determined opportunities and constraints, psychological motivation may be important in mobility processes as compensation for low parental status (Shanahan 2000). However, sociological research to date has not given much attention to the impact of motivational resources, other than educational plans, on educational attainment, nor whether this impact differs by adolescents’ alternative resources. Building on previous research on status attainment and the gendered life course, two central questions motivated this study: (1) Do the odds of graduation from college depend on adolescent motivation in a recent American cohort? (2) Is the effect of adolescent motivation on higher educational attainment moderated by social class and gender? To answer these questions, this study examines the effect of a multidimensional motivational construct, encompassing educational plans, academic self-concept, economic self-efficacy, and mastery, on college graduation and whether its effect is moderated by parental education and gender. These analyses increase understanding of the intergenerational transmission of inequality and point to areas for potential policy intervention.

### Social Reproduction and Status Attainment

Social theorists posit a universal, overriding parental interest in preserving class position intergenerationally (Breen and Goldthorpe 1997). That is, parents want their children to be at least as successful as themselves, and preferably more so. Those in the highest social class positions strive to enable their children to remain in this class; parents at lower levels develop strategies to assure that their children will either remain at the same level as themselves or attain higher positions. Since education is key to placement in the stratified occupational structure in modern societies, the interest in status preservation or increase, and especially a strong aversion to downward mobility, are key to understanding youth’s departure from school or advancement to higher educational levels once compulsory education is complete. Other scholars point out that social and cultural capital transmitted by students’ families produce differential capacity to navigate successful educational pathways (Crosnoe and Brenner 2016; Lareau 2003). Still, parental education is predictive, not strictly determinative, of children’s educational attainment. Among cohorts born in the 1980s, 50 percent of children of college-educated parents will earn a bachelor’s degree compared to about 20 percent of children of high school or community college-educated parents, and 10 percent of children whose parents did not graduate from high school (Ferrare 2016).

Whereas some countries have highly stratified educational systems that sort secondary students into tracks according to early aptitude (Kerckhoff 2001), America’s educational system allows for more mobility as students’ futures are not so strongly determined at an early age. However, it also inserts greater uncertainty with respect to future attainments, perhaps giving rise to special advantage to those with more fully developed achievement-related motivations (Mortimer and Krüger 2000). Motivational resources are more effective when structures are flexible, enabling movement between tracks, and fresh starts when initial trajectories are unpromising (Schoon and Heckhausen 2019).

The Wisconsin model of status attainment (Sewell, Haller, and Ohlendorf 1970; Sewell, Haller, and Portes 1969) was the most influential sociological framework for thinking about the social psychology of attainment in the 1970s and 1980s. This model posited that parents of higher socio-economic status have higher educational goals for their children and encourage them to seek high levels of education; children’s ensuing ambitious educational plans promote school achievement and educational attainment. Contemporary studies of educational attainment feature parental socioeconomic status, demographic characteristics, and family resources that foster attainment (Song and Mare 2017) and subjective reactions to mobility (Loveday 2015).

### Psychological Resources and Life Course Outcomes

While educational plans continue to be a central psychological resource in theoretical models of status attainment, other motivational constructs have been identified as predictors of important life course outcomes. The academic self-concept captures an adolescents’ subjective estimation of capacity to succeed in educational pursuits. Academic self-concepts may result from actual ability and school achievement (Chowdry, Crawford, and Goodman 2011), as well as from the reflected appraisals of significant others, especially parents and teachers. The academic self-concept, unlike global self-esteem, has significant positive reciprocal associations with grades in school and educational attainment (Marsh and O’Mara 2008).

Economic self-efficacy may also be a key resource for educational attainment. Individuals with high economic self-efficacy anticipate success in this sphere. Given the fact that economic achievement is highly dependent on educational attainment, high school students with stronger economic efficacy beliefs are found to have higher educational expectations and to take more steps to prepare for college admission (Grabowski et al. 2001). Moreover, adolescent economic self-efficacy predicts educational attainment, income, and financial independence in early adulthood (Burger et al. 2020).

Finally, mastery reflects the general belief that one can determine life outcomes and achieve one’s goals (Pearlin and Schooler 1978). This belief may be of great benefit in surmounting educational challenges. Individuals who have a stronger sense of mastery cope with stress in more constructive ways (Pearlin et al. 1981). Considering that pursuing higher education is frequently a stressful endeavor, it is unsurprising that previous longitudinal studies have linked mastery to educational attainment (Flouri 2006).

### Educational Mobility

In both classic and contemporary studies, far more attention has been directed to social class reproduction, the mechanisms producing stability of social class across generations, than to personal attributes or experiences that foster upward or downward mobility. Individual socioeconomic origins are thought to entail powerful advantages (or disadvantages) that perpetuate the existing class structure. Parents at higher levels of the class structure are advantaged in assuring their children’s favorable social class placement because they more easily bear the financial costs of post-secondary education (Breen and Goldthorpe 1997). Moreover, Bourdieu (1997) posits that cultural capital, a prime resource for achievement, is developed over a long period of time through children’s observations of, and interactions with, parents. The class-differentiated habitus (Bourdieu 1977) continues to be reinforced by experiences over a lifetime. Similarly, social class specific patterns of child rearing position the second generation for varying levels of success (Lareau 2003).

Clearly, such socialization-based models are less able to explain discontinuity in socio-economic status across generations or mobility, that is, why some children of lower-status parents become high-status adults. Life course scholars have addressed this shortcoming by conceptualizing human lives as projects that individuals participate in creating, producing “turning points” that depart from expected trajectories. According to Elder (1998:4), “individuals construct their own life course through the choices and actions they take within the opportunities and constraints of history and social circumstances.” Thus, social contexts determine which choices are available, but individual differences, including genetic propensity, cognitive skills, attitudes and physical ability, may also partially determine a person’s life chances. This study examines whether individual differences in adolescent motivation predict variability in adult educational attainment.

Adolescence is a formative life course stage situated at the precipice of the transition to adulthood when most educational attainment occurs. This makes it a highly relevant period to assess class differences in the impacts of motivational resources on higher educational attainment. Because students whose parents graduated from college are likely to have many advantages (e.g., social and cultural capital, their parents’ financial resources, successful parental role models, and useful parental guidance when they encounter educational hurdles), their success in the higher educational system might be considered overdetermined. Because first-generation college students do not have such advantages, psychological motivations that promote educational achievement may be particularly influential in their capacity to earn a college degree. Individual motivational attributes can overcome SES location and other structural dimensions in attaining upward mobility because actors can (to various degrees) select their social context and affect their behaviors within that context (Schoon and Heckhausen 2019).

### Educational Attainment and Gender

The status attainment process is clearly a gendered trajectory (Schoon and Polek 2011). In recent decades, American women have made great strides in educational attainment (Buchmann, DiPrete, and McDaniel, 2008). Men consistently out-earned women in academia until 1982, when an equal proportion of bachelor’s degrees were conferred to men and women for the first time in U.S. history (Buchmann and DiPrete 2006). Since then a new gap has emerged with women currently receiving more degrees than men. This monumental shift was partially due to the growing economic and occupational returns to education for women (Blossfeld et al. 2016). The increase in fatherless homes during this time, coupled with boys’ greater harm from an absent father, also contributed to girls’ growing educational advantage (Buchman and DiPrete 2006). Social capital differences are found to explain a large portion of the current female educational advantage (Klevan, Weinberg, and Middleton 2016). Women are more likely to have academically-oriented peer relationships and closer relationships with teachers. Parents now tend to have higher educational expectations for daughters than sons. Girls also exhibit stronger self-regulation, which enhances their educational achievement (Duckworth and Seligman 2006). While boys’ peer groups sometimes consider academic effort and success as undermining their masculinity (Legewie and DiPrete 2012), girls are unlikely to face such threat to their identity.

Despite an overall female advantage in higher education for recent cohorts, there is reason to believe that women may depend more than men on motivational resources to become upwardly mobile. Despite recent historical shifts in attitudes favoring gender equality, challenges remain. Women are still perceived as generally less competent than men and face stereotype threat, which heightens anxiety (Buchmann et al. 2008). To counter prevalent status expectations, they are called upon to prove their worth in educational and other settings, while men’s higher aptitude and skills are more often taken for granted (Ridgeway 2011). Gender bias in the classroom is prevalent, described as “a syntax of sexism so elusive that most teachers and students were completely unaware of its influence” (Sadker and Sadker 1995: 2). More recent work finds that boys still dominate classroom discussions (Sadker and Zittleman 2009). High school extracurricular activities are often highly sex-segregated (e.g., girls as cheerleaders, boys as football players), which highlight gender difference and are found to narrow perceived career options, i.e., plans to major in STEM fields in college (Legewie and DiPrete 2014). College women are more likely than men to experience multiple stressors, including doubts about their academic ability (Sax 2007), perceived barriers to careers (Luzzo and McWhirtle 2001), and heightened familial and financial burdens (Brougham et al. 2009).

Although gender norms have changed dramatically in recent decades in favor of equality and increasing acceptability of diverse life styles, most young people still expect to marry and to have children, and responsibility for home and childcare still disproportionately rests on women. Indicating that girls acknowledge these realities, one study found that female high school students with high educational and occupational aspirations expected to form families (marry and have children) later than those with lower, more traditional, aspirations (Johnson and Mortimer 2000). This “serial strategy,” enabling the completion of education and career establishment before family formation, could reduce work and family conflict. Boys showed no such pattern, i.e., family plans were unrelated to their occupational aspirations. This study suggests that girls’ achievement-related goals, as well as other motivational resources (e.g., promoting psychological engagement in the attainment process), may be more important for their eventual educational success and mobility than those of boys.

Finally, since women face “glass ceilings” and restricted entry to the more prestigious and lucrative male-dominated occupations and professions, their motivational resources may be more important than those of men both for higher educational attainment (qualifying them for entry-level positions), and for subsequent socioeconomic success. Whereas men more easily move into such desirable positions, their eventual success in these and other occupations may be more dependent on factors besides their educational degrees (e.g., prior work experience, contact networks, accomplishments after completing education), rendering them less consequential for educational and occupational attainment. Women receive higher income returns for college completion than men (DePrete and Buchmann 2006), who have these other routes to occupational and economic success. Consequently, women with low levels of motivation may be less likely to finish college and less likely to become upwardly mobile than men; conversely, women may receive greater benefit in higher education from enhanced motivation.

### Resource Substitution Theory

Some prior research has demonstrated the usefulness of adolescent motivational assets in predicting attainment outcomes (e.g., Hitlin and Johnson 2015). However, relatively little attention has been given to the question: under what conditions and for whom might such psychological assets be more or less important? As noted above, gender, a highly salient identity that critically shapes the life course, may moderate mobility processes. Social class may also moderate the impact of adolescent motivation on future achievement.

The theoretical distinction between resource substitution and resource multiplication effects is clearly relevant to these concerns (Ross and Mirowsky 2006). Resource substitution occurs when one resource, i.e., in this study, high levels of motivation, can substitute for another (parental socioeconomic status or male gender) in achieving desired end states. Resource multiplication occurs when two (or more) resources have cumulative effects; that is, the best outcomes occur when individuals possess both (or more) resources. Children of poorly resourced parents may depend more on personal assets to attain high status, indicating a resource substitution effect; alternatively, privileged children may be better equipped to accomplish their goals, indicating a resource multiplication effect. Women’s motivational resources could possibly compensate for their gender-related disadvantages (resource substitution), but men could possibly be doubly advantaged when they have both strong motivation and high social class origins. Given unequal opportunity structures and attainment pathways, it is worthwhile to investigate whether adolescent motivation involves a process of resource substitution, resource multiplication, or possibly has no significant influence (once potentially confounding variables are controlled) on higher educational attainment, and whether the impacts of motivation may differ by social class and gender.

## Current Study

Previous research has clearly demonstrated the valuable contribution of adolescent educational plans to adult educational attainment. However, status attainment research has not yet investigated the impact of other motivational resources that have been highlighted by life course scholars in recent decades. There is also a lack of consideration regarding how the effect of motivation on future attainment may differ between adolescents of different gender or social class background. The current study was designed to fill this gap. Based on previous research showing that multiple psychological resources predict important life course outcomes, this study hypothesizes that a latent motivational construct, reflecting educational plans, self-concept of ability, economic self-efficacy and mastery, is significantly and positively associated with earning a college degree independent of the effects of family background and adolescent academic success (Hypothesis 1). In the main analysis, rather than considering each of these four facets independently, or pitting them against one another in a multivariable model, their common variance is extracted and its implications for higher educational attainment is examined. Drawing from resource substitution and resource multiplication theory, this study further hypothesizes that the effect of adolescent motivation on college degree attainment differs across groups defined by parental education and gender (Hypothesis 2).

## Methods

### Sample

Data for this study come from the Youth Development Study (YDS). The YDS began with a random sample of 1,010 ninth-grade students in public high schools in St. Paul, Minnesota in spring 1988. The cohort was surveyed annually via in-school paper surveys (or mailed surveys, if the student had left the district or dropped out) through their senior year. Thereafter, the cohort was surveyed by mail 15 more times through 2011. In addition to surveying the youth, parents were invited to complete a survey in 1988 and 1991 to collect data on family background. This study used information reported by study participants as adolescents (1988 through 1991), their parents (1988 or 1991), and themselves as adults (2000 through 2011).

Some participants were eliminated from the analytic sample. To maximize sample size, all participants were retained who reported educational attainment at least once during the eight surveys fielded between 2000 and 2011, when participants were approximately aged 26–27 and 37–38 respectively. One hundred YDS subjects (9.9 percent of the original cohort) did not respond to any of these adult surveys. These participants had to be dropped because their adult educational attainment, the dependent variable, was not observed. Study attrition was higher among males and young adults of color. Importantly, attrition was not predicted by any of the first- or second-order motivational resources described further below. Additionally, approximately five percent of the original cohort did not have a parent who responded to a survey. These participants were dropped from the sample because their parents’ educational attainment, a potential moderating variable in this study, could not be observed. Finally, four additional participants were removed from the sample because they did not respond to the questions in the adolescent surveys that measure the main independent variable, adolescent motivational resources. Taken together, these restrictions yielded 874 cases to perform the analysis, representing 86.5 percent of the original sample. A statistical description of the sample is provided in Table 1.

### Outcome Measure

#### Adult educational attainment.

The dependent variable in all statistical models was adult educational attainment. To maximize the number of participants observed in adulthood, the most recent valid measure of education reported by the YDS cohort between 2000 and 2011 was used. Because of the significant value of a college degree, educational attainment was dichotomized as bachelor’s degree or above (32.0 percent) versus some college or less (68.0 percent).

### Adolescent Motivational Measures

Motivation, the key independent variable, is conceptualized as a multi-dimensional construct reflecting educational plans, academic self-concept, economic self-efficacy, and mastery. Educational plans were directly measured in the survey by a single question. The remaining first-order factors were latent variables measured by multiple indicators. The specific wording of each indicator is displayed in the appendix. Each motivational resource variable was measured during the second survey wave when youth were in the 10 th-grade. Measures from 11 th- or 12 th-grade were substituted whenever the earlier measure was missing. Mean and standard deviations of each indicator are presented in Table 1. Pairwise correlations between indicators are presented in Table 2. As expected, correlations between indicators within each latent factor were stronger than correlations between indicators across different latent factors.

#### Educational plans.

Youth were asked how much schooling they planned to complete. Responses ranged from “less than a high school degree” (coded 1) to “PhD or professional degree” (coded 6). This variable was treated as a continuous measure in the analysis.

#### Academic self-concept.

Youth were asked to rate their intelligence, reading ability, and overall school ability compared with their peers. Responses ranged from “far below average” (coded 1) to “far above average” (coded 2). Cronbach’s alpha for this construct was 0.73.

#### Economic self-efficacy.

Youth were asked to assess the chances that in the future they would have a job that pays well, own their own home, and have a job they enjoy doing. Responses ranged from “very low” (coded 1) to “very high” (coded 5). Cronbach’s alpha for this construct was 0.80.

#### Mastery.

Youth were asked how strongly they agree or disagree with six statements such as “_There is really no way I can solve some of the problems I have_”, and “_I can do just about anything I really set my mind to_”. Responses ranged from “strongly disagree” (coded 1) to “strongly agree” (coded 4). When appropriate, response values were reverse-coded so that a high number indicates a greater sense of control over one’s environment. Cronbach’s alpha for this construct was 0.77.

### Moderating Variables

#### Gender.

Gender was reported by the YDS participants in the first wave as male (45.2 percent) or female (54.8 percent).

#### Parental education.

Parental education was reported by the parents in 1988. In cases where two parents completed the survey, the higher reported educational attainment was used.1 To reduce the number of estimated interaction terms in the models, parental education was dichotomized as a bachelor’s degree or above (29.9 percent) versus some college or less (70.1 percent).

### Control Variables

While some studies attempt to analyze the pathways that link family social status, adolescent orientations, and adult attainment, the effect of adolescents’ motivational resources net of other precursors was the focus of this study. To estimate this independent effect, several variables measured in the parent survey were controlled.

#### Socio-demographic characteristics.

Family structure indicates whether the YDS adolescent lived with both biological/adoptive parents (56.6 percent), a stepfamily (14.0 percent), or in some other arrangement (usually single parent, 29.4 percent). Parental income was originally reported in 13 ordinal categories ranging from “under $5,000” to “$100,000 or more.” Income was recoded by assigning the midpoint of each category, and then transformed into a logarithmic scale (mean=10.3). Race was reported by the YDS participant in the first wave. Because of the small number of minority youth in the YDS, the race variable is a dichotomous indicator of non-Hispanic White (77.5 percent) versus all others (22.5 percent).

#### Parental expectations.

Parental expectations for youth’s educational achievement was measured on a scale ranging from “less than high school” (coded as 1) to “PhD or professional degree” (coded as 8). Each of these variables was measured at the first wave when the youth were in 9 th-grade. For some youth, both mothers and fathers responded to the survey. In these instances, the higher reported value of each parental variable was used. If a measure was missing in the first parent survey conducted in 1988, the measure from the second parent survey in 1991 was substituted.

#### Grade point average.

GPA is a proxy measure of youth’s ability to achieve in school. It was reported by youth in 1989, though measures from 1990 or 1991 were substituted when the earlier measure was not available. Controlling for this measure facilitates estimating the effect of adolescent motivation independent of differences in early academic success. The mean GPA for the sample was 7.8 on a 12-point scale, indicating approximately a C+ average.

### Missing Data

After filling in missing variables with data from subsequent waves, a small amount of missingness on control variables remained. This ranged from one missing observation of parental expectations (0.1 percent of the sample) to 19 missing observations of GPA (2.2 percent of the sample). To retain as many cases as possible, missing values were imputed using the Multiple Imputation with Chained Equations (MICE) command in Stata. This method produces less biased estimates than listwise deletion provided that the data are missing at random (Little and Rubin 2002).2

### Statistical Analysis

The analysis began with a second-order confirmatory factor analysis (Bollen 1989) to test the validity of the hypothesized model in which adolescent “motivation” is constructed from educational plans, academic self-concept, economic self-efficacy, and mastery. Significant correlation was found between nearly every pair of indicators used to construct these first-order variables (presented in Table 2, which bolstered the hypothesis that they were related and could constitute a second-order latent factor. All models were estimated using Stata 15. After estimating the second-order motivation variable, values of motivation were predicted for each participant in the sample.

Next, the association between adolescent motivation and college graduation was estimated using logistic regression. The log odds of college graduation were modelled as a function of the control variables plus the motivation construct. Additional models tested whether the effect of motivation on college graduation was moderated by parental education and gender using two- and three-way interaction terms.

As a supplementary analysis, college graduation was predicted using the first-order latent motivational resources. This was a way to discern whether results from the main analysis were largely driven by certain dimensions of the second-order variable. To estimate heterogenous effects, separate models were also estimated with subsamples split by parental education and gender.

## Results

### Confirmatory Factor Analysis

The confirmatory factor analysis supported the conceptualization of a multi-dimensional motivational resource factor. Figure 1 displays the second-order factor model with standardized coefficients. A latent motivation variable was strongly related to educational plans and the three first-order latent variables: academic self-concept, economic self-efficacy, and mastery. The coefficients for each pathway in the model were statistically significant (p<0.001). Model fit is considered acceptable when the root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) is below 0.06 and the comparative fit index (CFI) is greater than 0.90 (Kline 2011). The model had an RMSEA of 0.048 and CFI of 0.96, suggesting good fit to the data.

A value of the second-order latent motivation construct was computed for each person in the sample. Levels of motivation varied significantly across the two moderating factors: parental education and gender. This is visualized in Figure 2. Children of college graduates reported higher levels of motivation on average than children whose parents did not go as far in school (p<.001). Female adolescents reported lower motivation on average than male adolescents (p<.05). However, sex differences were not significant within each level of parental education.

### Regression Analysis

Next, the effect of the latent motivation construct on college graduation was examined. Estimated coefficients are presented in Table 3 In the first model, including only the control variables, adult college graduation was positively related to parental college graduation (OR=2.926, p<.001), parental expectations for the adolescent’s education (OR=1.515, p<.001), and the adolescent’s grade point average (OR=1.487, p<.001). Adolescents living in stepfamilies were somewhat less likely to complete a bachelor’s degree than those living in two-parent intact families, though this estimate was only of borderline significance (OR=0.601, p<0.1). Parental income, race, and gender showed no significant independent association with college completion. Although women in the United States currently outpace men in college degree attainment, this difference was not as pronounced for this cohort.

In Model 2, the motivation construct, standardized to have a mean of zero and standard deviation of one, was added. As hypothesized, higher levels of motivation predicted greater odds of college graduation (OR=1.622, p<0.001). The estimated effects of parental expectations and GPA were slightly attenuated between the first and second models, indicating that adolescent motivation partially mediates the effect of these factors on future educational attainment. Interestingly, the estimated effect of female gender increased in magnitude and approached statistical significance (OR=1.391, p<0.1) after controlling for motivation. This suggests that lower levels of motivation for female compared to male adolescents is partially responsible for depressing female educational attainment in this cohort.

Neither parental education nor gender were significant moderators of the effect of motivation on college graduation in the whole sample, evidenced by the non-significant interaction terms in Models 3 and 4. However, including the three-way interaction term in Model 5 showed that there was some heterogeneity across groups when stratified by parental education and gender. The main effect of motivation in Model 5 represents the effect for male adolescents whose parents did not complete college. For this group, levels of motivation were not significantly associated with odds of college graduation, indicating that motivation does not enhance educational mobility among males. The significant Motivation*Female term (OR=1.656, p<0.05) indicates that motivation had a stronger positive effect on college graduation for females than for males when parents did not graduate from college. Other interaction terms were not significant.

To aid interpretation of these findings, the predicted probabilities of college graduation by gender, parental education, and motivation level are shown in Figure 3. Among children of college graduates, higher levels of motivation predicted a steady increase in likelihood that they would also become college graduates. This effect was essentially the same for both men and women. However, there was a significant gender difference in the effect of motivation for achieving upward educational mobility. Female adolescents whose parents did not graduate from college received a significant boost in their likelihood of earning a bachelor’s degree at higher levels of motivation. However, among male adolescents with less-educated parents, the slope of the line was flat. Even at two standard deviations above the mean level of motivation, the probability that a male adolescent would earn a bachelor’s degree if his parents did not was approximately one in five, compared to one in two for a female adolescent with similarly-educated parents or seven in ten for adolescents whose parents were college-educated.

### Supplementary Analysis

As a supplementary analysis, the effects of each of the first-order motivational resources on college graduation were estimated for the whole sample and for subgroups defined by parental education and gender. These models help to identify the specific motivational resource that could be more consequential in determining educational attainment. Each motivational resource was standardized to have a mean of zero and standard deviation of one. In Table 4, the first model shows estimates for the full sample, including parental education, gender, and the control variables. Here, both educational plans (OR=1.535, p<0.01) and academic self-concept (OR=1.532, p<0.001) had significant positive effects on college graduation. Economic self-efficacy and mastery had no significant independent effect net of the other factors in the model.

Comparing effect magnitudes and significance across gender and parental education categories yields interesting insights. Among male adolescents whose parents were not college graduates (Model 2), none of the motivational resources significantly predicted odds of earning a bachelor’s degree. This finding coheres with the main analysis using the second-order latent variable. Among female adolescents of non-college graduates (Model 3), academic self-concept appeared to be the driving factor producing upward educational mobility (OR=2.186, p<0.001), while the effect of educational plans was only of borderline significance (OR=1.492, p<0.1). Among male children of college-graduates (Model 4), the effect of educational plans was positive and borderline significant (OR=2.131, p<0.1) for earning a bachelor’s degree, while the effects of the other agentic resources were null. Educational plans also appeared instrumental in enabling female children of college-graduates (Model 5) to attain the same level of education as their parents (OR=2.657, p<0.01). In summary, these models suggest that educational plans were the most important psychological resource for children of college graduates to attain the same high level of education as their parents, while academic self-concept was more important for female adolescents to experience upward educational mobility.

## Discussion

Both life course scholars and developmental psychologists consider the human capacity to set goals, and to act purposefully within networks of opportunity and constraint to achieve them, are critical to the understanding of life trajectories and life-span development. The present study aimed to investigate the role of adolescent motivational resources in higher educational attainment, and whether their impacts were moderated by social class and gender. Consistent with the assumption that parents, as well as their adolescent children, would be motivated to exceed the status of the family of origin (Breen and Goldthorpe 1997), special interest was directed toward investigating why some youth were able to attain college degrees despite having parents who did not.

As described in the introduction, this research was initially inspired to address deficiency in the sociological study of attainment, but not surprisingly, due to the preoccupation with similar questions in developmental psychology, its contribution extends across disciplines. Like life course sociologists, developmental psychologists are interested in how motivational resources guide human effort and behavior and engender varying levels of adaptation and success. According to the “motivational theory of life-span development” (Heckhausen and Buchmann 2019), life courses are shaped jointly by social structure and agency, with individual motivation and effort to pursue goals dependent on both expectancies and values (see also Eccles 2007). Individuals assess whether goal pursuit will be difficult and their likelihood of success based on their assessments of their individual abilities and capacities (e.g., the extent to which they can control life outcomes). Importantly, according to this theory, location in the structure of inequality affects the resources available to navigate chosen paths and the degree of uncertainty and unpredictability likely to be confronted. Those of lower status need “compensatory advantages” to achieve upward mobility, including greater commitment to goals and stronger personal control perceptions (Heckhausen and Buchmann 2019).

As in this study, developmental psychologists have considered the extent to which various dimensions of motivation vary by socio-economic status and gender; the impacts of motivational orientations and beliefs on future expectations, adjustment and educational success; and whether they have distinct effects depending on the person’s structural location. A key question for developmental scholars, as here, is whether motivational resources can overcome the disadvantages associated with structural location (Haase et al. 2008; Heckhausen and Chang 2009), including social class and gender. For example, is locus of control a potential resource that can compensate for background disadvantages, enabling youth to obtain success “against the odds”? In one study (Ng-Knight and Schoon 2017), internal control was found to be protective against short-term experiences of NEET (not in education, employment or training) for those from lower socioeconomic backgrounds, supporting the resource substitution hypothesis. It had no impact on the time spent NEET for those from middle and high socio-economic backgrounds. Moreover, goal engagement has been found to be a more powerful predictor of apprenticeship placement for German adolescent girls than for boys (Haase et al. 2008).

The present study has pursued many of the same questions. As expected, a multidimensional motivational construct predicted youth’ ability to graduate from college as adults. This effect was equally strong for children of college graduates and those whose parents had less education. In accord with predictions based on previous research, these findings demonstrate that relatively high levels of motivation give youth without college-educated parents an advantage with respect to college graduation in the relatively open and unstructured American educational system (Heckhausen and Chang 2009; Schoon and Heckhausen 2019). They also indicate that the impacts of motivational resources on attainment adheres to a “resource substitution” pattern (Ross and Mirowsky 2006); that is, high levels of achievement-related motivation can compensate for the absence of a college-educated parent in achieving college degrees.

The results also demonstrate substantial gender heterogeneity in the power of adolescent motivation to predict upward mobility. Women depended significantly more than men on this psychological resource to achieve college graduation. This may be surprising, considering the substantial female advantage in higher education that has emerged in recent decades. Three plausible reasons could explain this finding, but selection of the most compelling awaits further research. First, as previously alluded, women with high aspirations face challenges given traditional, albeit changing, work and family roles that mitigate against high occupational achievement. More often than their male counterparts, women must figure out how to meet conflicting expectations (i.e., related to educational attainment, work and parenthood). These may place a premium on adolescent motivational resources both in anticipating and developing strategies to minimize such conflict, and in achieving the higher levels of educational attainment needed to gain entry to higher status occupational positions.

Second, women tend to experience higher levels of stress in college than men (Brougham et al. 2009; Sax 2007) and must draw on motivational resources to counteract such stress. Gendered norms may make balancing family responsibilities with scholastic achievement more difficult for women, especially those in the sample who are first-generation college students. Relatedly, the findings point to gender differences in self-assessment that have consequences for educational attainment. Despite the fact that women tend to outperform men in academics, they internalize stereotypical ideas about deficiency in their abilities and likely task performance (Correll 2001). By contrast, if men report high levels of confidence (as indicated by their mastery, economic self-efficacy, high academic self-concepts and educational plans) irrespective of their underlying capacities, it would stand to reason that increases in reported motivational resources do not necessarily translate to increases in men’s future attainment.

A third interpretation relates to gendered differences in the “return” to higher education (DiPrete and Buchmann 2006). Men and women both have better occupational prospects with a college degree than without one. However, men without a college degree have better prospects than women without a college degree. Therefore, if a man and woman both have high occupational aspirations, the man has a better chance of fulfilling these aspirations without a college degree than the woman does. College is the key pathway toward success for women, while men have alternative options. This might explain why increases in motivation are more closely tied to educational mobility for women than men.

There are several limitations to this research. The first relates to the historical context. This study recounts the experience of educational mobility in a cohort born in the early 1970’s (Gen X in popular parlance). The YDS cohort graduated from high school in 1991 and likely attended college (if they did attend) in the mid-1990s. The female advantage in higher education was not as pronounced then as it is currently, and women in that cohort may have depended more on high levels of motivation to achieve upward mobility than more recent cohorts. Moreover, these youth came of age at a time of educational and economic expansion. The “hollowing out” of the middle class, the increasingly lengthy and precarious transition from school to work, and declining opportunity for those without college degrees have made it incumbent on all youth to strive to graduate from college. Under these circumstances, educational plans and related motivational orientations may have become less consequential for attainment for more recent youth cohorts.

Second, the YDS cohort is not nationally representative. It is a sample of youth from St. Paul, Minnesota, a state with somewhat higher average levels of college completion than the rest of the United States. Therefore, those wanting to generalize these findings to the whole country should proceed with caution. Third, since the panel was drawn from a largely White city, there are not enough cases to do more fine-grained comparisons across race and gender groups. Finally, there is the risk of omitted variable bias as in all observational studies. Motivational orientations are complex phenomena influenced by perhaps countless social relationships and contingencies. It cannot be ruled out that the longitudinal associations observed here would be rendered spurious by including some unmeasured variable. A more stringent test would be to compare the effects of adolescent motivation on adult outcomes for children clustered within schools or families. This was not possible with YDS data.

Despite these limitations, the present study enhances understanding of individual lives. Confirming and extending recent research in developmental psychology, it focuses explicitly on educational attainment and social mobility and centers motivation as a significant resource for overcoming disadvantaged backgrounds. Unlike prior research in sociology focused on plans and aspirations, this study examined three other psychological achievement-related variables included in a multidimensional latent construct. Research in developmental psychology also tends to focus on psychological resources, one at a time. The educational mobility process was found to be gendered, with women’s success more dependent on motivational resources than that of men. This finding is noteworthy given the current context of female advantage in higher education.

This research also has implications for social policy. Those who are concerned about inequality typically focus on dismantling structural barriers that hinder people’s success. This work is important and must continue. However, in addition to making the pathways to and through higher education easier to travel, it is vital to also consider how to increase youth’s motivation to select and persevere in their educational pathways. Educational inequality is a multi-level process involving (but not limited to) differences in school context and resources as well as students’ individual motivation and abilities. Reforms that aim to address multiple levels of causation will likely be more effective than singular interventions in reducing intergenerational social reproduction and inequality.

## Conclusion

The results of this study promote understanding of the adolescent psychological resources that facilitate future educational attainment. In contrast with previous studies, adolescent motivation was conceptualized as a multidimensional latent construct and used to estimate the heterogenous impact of motivational resources on future attainment by gender and social class. The results suggest that adolescents with high levels of motivation were significantly more likely than their peers to graduate from college. Females whose parents did not graduate from college were particularly advantaged by strong motivational resources. For them, higher educational attainment was largely driven by the academic self-concept, whereas educational plans heightened the attainment of students whose parents graduated from college. Surprisingly, the motivational resources considered here did not influence the probability of college graduation among male children of less-educated parents. These findings suggest that more resources should be devoted to interventions that enhance the adolescent psychological resources that promote educational success. However, it is important to recognize that such strategies may not produce equitable results. More research is needed to identify the reasons why higher levels of motivation did not facilitate upward mobility among male adolescents.

# Believing and Achieving: Gendered Pathways Toward Upward Educational Mobility in the United States
