![Image 13: Students line up to receive their diplomas during a graduation ceremony at sunset in Santa Monica, California, June 2013. (Getty/Los Angeles Times/Allen J. Schaben)](https://www.americanprogress.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2021/04/AttainmentGapsColumn.jpg?w=1040)

Students line up to receive their diplomas during a graduation ceremony at sunset in Santa Monica, California, June 2013. (Getty/Los Angeles Times/Allen J. Schaben)

For the first time ever, half of the young adults in the United States have earned a college degree. From 2009 to 2019, the share of adults between the ages of 25 and 34 who earned an associate degree or higher rose from [41 percent](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/2009/demo/educational-attainment/p20-566.html) to [50 percent](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/2019/demo/educational-attainment/cps-detailed-tables.html). In 2017, the last time the Center for American Progress evaluated national attainment, degree attainment was [just below the 50 percent mark](https://americanprogress.org/issues/education-postsecondary/news/2018/04/18/449758/good-bad-news-college-attainment-trends/). While hitting this milestone is good news and increases have occurred across demographic groups, there hasn’t been a great deal of progress in closing large and persistent racial equity gaps.

Closing these gaps must be a high priority for the Biden administration, states, and colleges as they seek to build a more educated nation. Over the past decade, Black and Latino young adults experienced the most dramatic growth in attainment; but they also started off with the lowest attainment rates compared with other racial or ethnic groups, and they remain the least likely to earn a college degree. Moreover, the attainment rates among Black and Latino men are even lower.

These alarming equity gaps in attainment exist because of [structural inequities](https://americanprogress.org/issues/race/reports/2019/08/07/472910/systematic-inequality-economic-opportunity/) in our society, including the [education system](https://edtrustmain.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/09/14161442/Hard-Truths-Why-Only-Race-Conscious-Policies-Can-Fix-Racism-in-Higher-Education-January-2020.pdf), which consistently fails to serve Black and Latino adults. Unfortunately, the pandemic is expected to only [exacerbate](https://www.thirdway.org/infographic/covid-19s-impact-on-black-college-students) these educational gaps. This spring semester, undergraduate enrollment [decreased by 4.5 percent](https://www.insidehighered.com/news/2021/03/11/colleges-continue-losing-undergraduate-enrollment-spring-even-graduate-enrollment?utm_source=Inside+Higher+Ed&utm_campaign=fdb9f7b95f-DNU_2021_COPY_02&utm_medium=email&utm_term=0_1fcbc04421-fdb9f7b95f-235163529&mc_cid=fdb9f7b95f&mc_eid=e0ae31a60f), with larger declines among Black, Latino, and Native American populations. Community college enrollment took the hardest hit, especially [among men](https://www.newamerica.org/education-policy/edcentral/where-did-all-the-community-college-students-go-2/), while [enrollment at for-profit institutions](https://www.insidehighered.com/news/2021/03/11/colleges-continue-losing-undergraduate-enrollment-spring-even-graduate-enrollment?utm_source=Inside+Higher+Ed&utm_campaign=fdb9f7b95f-DNU_2021_COPY_02&utm_medium=email&utm_term=0_1fcbc04421-fdb9f7b95f-235163529&mc_cid=fdb9f7b95f&mc_eid=e0ae31a60f) increased throughout the pandemic.

Previous administrations have focused on [increasing overall attainment](https://www.ed.gov/sites/default/files/winning-the-future.ppt), but that hasn’t proved effective at tackling racial equity gaps. The Biden administration’s pledge to [advance racial equity](https://joebiden.com/racial-economic-equity/) in postsecondary education is a perfect opportunity to dedicate resources to close attainment gaps by race and gender. For example, the U.S. Department of Education should explore options for conducting [equity](https://americanprogress.org/issues/education-postsecondary/news/2021/02/03/495334/biden-administration-can-now-make-college-affordable-accountable-racially-just/)[audits](https://americanprogress.org/issues/education-postsecondary/news/2019/04/03/465193/equity-audits-tool-campus-improvement/) to identify barriers to completion at the institutional level, as well as ways that colleges can improve outcomes for racially underrepresented students. Congress and states, meanwhile, should help close attainment gaps by eliminating funding disparities at [institutions serving](https://americanprogress.org/issues/education-postsecondary/reports/2020/10/07/491242/78-billion-community-college-funding-shortfall/)[larger proportions](https://americanprogress.org/issues/education-postsecondary/news/2020/12/08/492883/hispanic-serving-institutions-need-1-billion-federal-funding/) of students of color. Finally, the new administration should seek to reengage students who left college without a degree by convening a commission of experts to identify the barriers contributing to student withdrawal—and making its findings public.

This column provides an update on attainment increases over the past decade and reveals how racial equity gaps persist. For this analysis, degree attainment is defined as the percentage of adults between the ages of 25 and 34 who have earned at least an associate degree or higher. This reflects an age range when people can expect to maximize the economic benefits of a degree over a longer period. CAP analyzed [2009](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/2009/demo/educational-attainment/p20-566.html) and [2019](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/2019/demo/educational-attainment/cps-detailed-tables.html) data from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey (CPS), which does not report attainment data for Native American adults, disaggregate among Asian American subpopulations, or report the attainment of postsecondary certificates.

It is important to put the change in attainment rates over that decade in context. For example, the population of young adult Latinos with a college degree rose 11 percentage points, compared with a 9 percentage point surge for white young adults. These increases may sound similar, but in fact, the change for Latinos is much more dramatic, because this demographic’s attainment rate was only 19 percent a decade ago, compared with 49 percent for whites. Indeed, Latinos experienced nearly a 60 percent jump in attainment, which represents an additional 1.3 million college-educated Latinos. Similarly, the percentage of Black men with a degree rose from 23 percent to 35 percent during this time frame, a jump of 50 percent that represents more than half a million additional Black men with a degree. These shifts represent a great deal of hard work on the part of individual students and their families to overcome significant barriers to earning a college degree. They also reflect some additional success on the part of the colleges and universities serving the students.

Still, there is much more work to be done by policymakers and institutions to allow these populations to share equally in the American dream, especially in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic.

### Latino and Black adults have the largest attainment growth but remain the least likely to earn a college degree

Since 2000, Latino undergraduate enrollment at degree-granting institutions [has increased](https://nces.ed.gov/pubs2020/2020144.pdf) more than that of other racial or ethnic groups. Latinos are also the [largest foreign-born group](https://www.census.gov/content/dam/Census/library/publications/2015/demo/p25-1143.pdf) and are projected to be the third-fastest-growing population in the United States. Their rising success translates into Latino adults having a nearly 60 percent increase in attainment—the largest growth of other racial or ethnic groups. (see Table 1) If this rate of change continues, almost half (49 percent) of Latino adults will be college-educated by 2029—an encouraging projection for Latino attainment. Understanding why Latino adults have experienced such substantial progress, at least before the pandemic, is a topic worthy of examination, especially in states with [sizable Latino populations](https://edtrust.org/the-equity-line/broken-mirrors-ii-how-many-latino-students-are-at-public-colleges-and-universities-not-as-many-as-there-should-be/) and postsecondary enrollment—for example, California, Florida, New York, and Texas.

Yet despite Latino adults having the largest attainment growth, they remain the least likely racial or ethnic group to earn a college degree. In fact, the share of Latino adults with a college degree (31 percent) trails the attainment rate of white adults by 27 percentage points. Since 2009, the Latino-white attainment gap has only slightly narrowed, closing by 2.5 percentage points. Also concerning are growing gaps by gender. Latino men remain the least likely to obtain a degree, at 26 percent, and the gap between Latina women and Latino men is widening.

**Table 1**

Meanwhile, since 2009, Black degree attainment has increased by more than 30 percent—the second-largest attainment growth of other racial or ethnic groups, translating to 978,000 more college-educated Black adults. If Black adults stay on that trajectory, half of them will be college-educated by 2029—an encouraging projection. But a large equity gap remains between Black and white degree attainment. The share of Black adults with a college degree (38 percent) lags the attainment of white adults by 19 percentage points, and the Black-white attainment gap only narrowed by 0.1 percentage points from 2009 to 2019. It is, however, encouraging that the gap between Black women and men has narrowed from 11 percentage points in 2009 to 6 percentage points in 2019. In fact, Black men have seen one of the greatest growths among all groups, with an 11.7 percentage point change.

### Reengaging students who left college without a degree can help improve attainment

Students who leave college without a degree are wasting time in school since they are not getting the workforce benefit of a postsecondary credential. These students are also [less likely](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED556472.pdf) than college completers to repay their student loan debt. The story is even more alarming among Black adults who do not finish college: [More than half](https://americanprogress.org/issues/education-postsecondary/reports/2019/12/02/477929/continued-student-loan-crisis-black-borrowers/) of Black noncompleters default on their student loans, compared with 3 percent of bachelor’s degree-holders and 13 percent of associate degree-holders who are Black. One way to close these equity gaps is to reengage students who do not complete.

In 2019, nearly [17 percent of young adults](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/2019/demo/educational-attainment/cps-detailed-tables.html), more than 7.5 million in total, left college without a degree. (see Figure 1) The issue of “some college, no degree” hits across racial groups, but the disparities are higher among Black and Latino adults. More than 22 percent of Black adults and nearly 18 percent of Latino adults leave college without a degree, compared with about 16 percent of their white peers and only 9 percent of Asian adults.

**Figure 1**

If the entire population of adults who left college without a credential in 2019 received a degree, more than two-thirds (67 percent) of the population would be college-educated, translating to more than 30.3 million people. This achievement would also spill over by race, with more than 60 percent of Black adults and nearly half of Latino adults being college-educated. However, even if this scenario were to occur, disparities by race and gender would narrow but still exist. Black adults would trail white adults in attainment by 13 percentage points, and the Latino-white attainment gap would be 25 percentage points.

### Conclusion

Despite some attainment progress across groups, large and persistent equity gaps remain. As the Biden administration works to build a more college-educated population, any measures to improve attainment should be designed above all to improve equity, targeting race and gender gaps and reengaging students who left college without a degree. The federal government and states share responsibility for equitably raising attainment. As mentioned earlier, Congress and states should close funding gaps at [institutions serving](https://americanprogress.org/issues/education-postsecondary/reports/2020/10/07/491242/78-billion-community-college-funding-shortfall/)[larger proportions](https://americanprogress.org/issues/education-postsecondary/news/2020/12/08/492883/hispanic-serving-institutions-need-1-billion-federal-funding/) of students of color. Meanwhile, the U.S. Department of Education should explore options for conducting [equity](https://americanprogress.org/issues/education-postsecondary/news/2021/02/03/495334/biden-administration-can-now-make-college-affordable-accountable-racially-just/)[audits](https://americanprogress.org/issues/education-postsecondary/news/2019/04/03/465193/equity-audits-tool-campus-improvement/) to identify ways that colleges can improve outcomes for racially underrepresented students; and the administration should convene a commission of experts to identify the barriers contributing to student withdrawal and make its findings public.

[Nearly two-thirds](https://cew.georgetown.edu/cew-reports/recovery-job-growth-and-education-requirements-through-2020/) of jobs now require some form of postsecondary education, so a college degree is necessary to participate in today’s economy. Closing racial equity gaps would be an effective way to help meet the administration’s promise to “[Build Back Better](https://joebiden.com/build-back-better/),” especially in the wake of the pandemic.

# Building a College-Educated America Requires Closing Racial Gaps in Attainment

Half of young adults have earned a college degree, yet large and persistent racial equity gaps remain.

*   Authors

![Image 13: Students line up to receive their diplomas during a graduation ceremony at sunset in Santa Monica, California, June 2013. (Getty/Los Angeles Times/Allen J. Schaben)](https://www.americanprogress.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2021/04/AttainmentGapsColumn.jpg?w=1040)

Students line up to receive their diplomas during a graduation ceremony at sunset in Santa Monica, California, June 2013. (Getty/Los Angeles Times/Allen J. Schaben)

For the first time ever, half of the young adults in the United States have earned a college degree. From 2009 to 2019, the share of adults between the ages of 25 and 34 who earned an associate degree or higher rose from [41 percent](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/2009/demo/educational-attainment/p20-566.html) to [50 percent](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/2019/demo/educational-attainment/cps-detailed-tables.html). In 2017, the last time the Center for American Progress evaluated national attainment, degree attainment was [just below the 50 percent mark](https://americanprogress.org/issues/education-postsecondary/news/2018/04/18/449758/good-bad-news-college-attainment-trends/). While hitting this milestone is good news and increases have occurred across demographic groups, there hasn’t been a great deal of progress in closing large and persistent racial equity gaps.

Closing these gaps must be a high priority for the Biden administration, states, and colleges as they seek to build a more educated nation. Over the past decade, Black and Latino young adults experienced the most dramatic growth in attainment; but they also started off with the lowest attainment rates compared with other racial or ethnic groups, and they remain the least likely to earn a college degree. Moreover, the attainment rates among Black and Latino men are even lower.

These alarming equity gaps in attainment exist because of [structural inequities](https://americanprogress.org/issues/race/reports/2019/08/07/472910/systematic-inequality-economic-opportunity/) in our society, including the [education system](https://edtrustmain.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/09/14161442/Hard-Truths-Why-Only-Race-Conscious-Policies-Can-Fix-Racism-in-Higher-Education-January-2020.pdf), which consistently fails to serve Black and Latino adults. Unfortunately, the pandemic is expected to only [exacerbate](https://www.thirdway.org/infographic/covid-19s-impact-on-black-college-students) these educational gaps. This spring semester, undergraduate enrollment [decreased by 4.5 percent](https://www.insidehighered.com/news/2021/03/11/colleges-continue-losing-undergraduate-enrollment-spring-even-graduate-enrollment?utm_source=Inside+Higher+Ed&utm_campaign=fdb9f7b95f-DNU_2021_COPY_02&utm_medium=email&utm_term=0_1fcbc04421-fdb9f7b95f-235163529&mc_cid=fdb9f7b95f&mc_eid=e0ae31a60f), with larger declines among Black, Latino, and Native American populations. Community college enrollment took the hardest hit, especially [among men](https://www.newamerica.org/education-policy/edcentral/where-did-all-the-community-college-students-go-2/), while [enrollment at for-profit institutions](https://www.insidehighered.com/news/2021/03/11/colleges-continue-losing-undergraduate-enrollment-spring-even-graduate-enrollment?utm_source=Inside+Higher+Ed&utm_campaign=fdb9f7b95f-DNU_2021_COPY_02&utm_medium=email&utm_term=0_1fcbc04421-fdb9f7b95f-235163529&mc_cid=fdb9f7b95f&mc_eid=e0ae31a60f) increased throughout the pandemic.

Previous administrations have focused on [increasing overall attainment](https://www.ed.gov/sites/default/files/winning-the-future.ppt), but that hasn’t proved effective at tackling racial equity gaps. The Biden administration’s pledge to [advance racial equity](https://joebiden.com/racial-economic-equity/) in postsecondary education is a perfect opportunity to dedicate resources to close attainment gaps by race and gender. For example, the U.S. Department of Education should explore options for conducting [equity](https://americanprogress.org/issues/education-postsecondary/news/2021/02/03/495334/biden-administration-can-now-make-college-affordable-accountable-racially-just/)[audits](https://americanprogress.org/issues/education-postsecondary/news/2019/04/03/465193/equity-audits-tool-campus-improvement/) to identify barriers to completion at the institutional level, as well as ways that colleges can improve outcomes for racially underrepresented students. Congress and states, meanwhile, should help close attainment gaps by eliminating funding disparities at [institutions serving](https://americanprogress.org/issues/education-postsecondary/reports/2020/10/07/491242/78-billion-community-college-funding-shortfall/)[larger proportions](https://americanprogress.org/issues/education-postsecondary/news/2020/12/08/492883/hispanic-serving-institutions-need-1-billion-federal-funding/) of students of color. Finally, the new administration should seek to reengage students who left college without a degree by convening a commission of experts to identify the barriers contributing to student withdrawal—and making its findings public.

This column provides an update on attainment increases over the past decade and reveals how racial equity gaps persist. For this analysis, degree attainment is defined as the percentage of adults between the ages of 25 and 34 who have earned at least an associate degree or higher. This reflects an age range when people can expect to maximize the economic benefits of a degree over a longer period. CAP analyzed [2009](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/2009/demo/educational-attainment/p20-566.html) and [2019](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/2019/demo/educational-attainment/cps-detailed-tables.html) data from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey (CPS), which does not report attainment data for Native American adults, disaggregate among Asian American subpopulations, or report the attainment of postsecondary certificates.

It is important to put the change in attainment rates over that decade in context. For example, the population of young adult Latinos with a college degree rose 11 percentage points, compared with a 9 percentage point surge for white young adults. These increases may sound similar, but in fact, the change for Latinos is much more dramatic, because this demographic’s attainment rate was only 19 percent a decade ago, compared with 49 percent for whites. Indeed, Latinos experienced nearly a 60 percent jump in attainment, which represents an additional 1.3 million college-educated Latinos. Similarly, the percentage of Black men with a degree rose from 23 percent to 35 percent during this time frame, a jump of 50 percent that represents more than half a million additional Black men with a degree. These shifts represent a great deal of hard work on the part of individual students and their families to overcome significant barriers to earning a college degree. They also reflect some additional success on the part of the colleges and universities serving the students.

Still, there is much more work to be done by policymakers and institutions to allow these populations to share equally in the American dream, especially in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic.

### Latino and Black adults have the largest attainment growth but remain the least likely to earn a college degree

Since 2000, Latino undergraduate enrollment at degree-granting institutions [has increased](https://nces.ed.gov/pubs2020/2020144.pdf) more than that of other racial or ethnic groups. Latinos are also the [largest foreign-born group](https://www.census.gov/content/dam/Census/library/publications/2015/demo/p25-1143.pdf) and are projected to be the third-fastest-growing population in the United States. Their rising success translates into Latino adults having a nearly 60 percent increase in attainment—the largest growth of other racial or ethnic groups. (see Table 1) If this rate of change continues, almost half (49 percent) of Latino adults will be college-educated by 2029—an encouraging projection for Latino attainment. Understanding why Latino adults have experienced such substantial progress, at least before the pandemic, is a topic worthy of examination, especially in states with [sizable Latino populations](https://edtrust.org/the-equity-line/broken-mirrors-ii-how-many-latino-students-are-at-public-colleges-and-universities-not-as-many-as-there-should-be/) and postsecondary enrollment—for example, California, Florida, New York, and Texas.

Yet despite Latino adults having the largest attainment growth, they remain the least likely racial or ethnic group to earn a college degree. In fact, the share of Latino adults with a college degree (31 percent) trails the attainment rate of white adults by 27 percentage points. Since 2009, the Latino-white attainment gap has only slightly narrowed, closing by 2.5 percentage points. Also concerning are growing gaps by gender. Latino men remain the least likely to obtain a degree, at 26 percent, and the gap between Latina women and Latino men is widening.

**Table 1**

Meanwhile, since 2009, Black degree attainment has increased by more than 30 percent—the second-largest attainment growth of other racial or ethnic groups, translating to 978,000 more college-educated Black adults. If Black adults stay on that trajectory, half of them will be college-educated by 2029—an encouraging projection. But a large equity gap remains between Black and white degree attainment. The share of Black adults with a college degree (38 percent) lags the attainment of white adults by 19 percentage points, and the Black-white attainment gap only narrowed by 0.1 percentage points from 2009 to 2019. It is, however, encouraging that the gap between Black women and men has narrowed from 11 percentage points in 2009 to 6 percentage points in 2019. In fact, Black men have seen one of the greatest growths among all groups, with an 11.7 percentage point change.

### Reengaging students who left college without a degree can help improve attainment

Students who leave college without a degree are wasting time in school since they are not getting the workforce benefit of a postsecondary credential. These students are also [less likely](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED556472.pdf) than college completers to repay their student loan debt. The story is even more alarming among Black adults who do not finish college: [More than half](https://americanprogress.org/issues/education-postsecondary/reports/2019/12/02/477929/continued-student-loan-crisis-black-borrowers/) of Black noncompleters default on their student loans, compared with 3 percent of bachelor’s degree-holders and 13 percent of associate degree-holders who are Black. One way to close these equity gaps is to reengage students who do not complete.

In 2019, nearly [17 percent of young adults](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/2019/demo/educational-attainment/cps-detailed-tables.html), more than 7.5 million in total, left college without a degree. (see Figure 1) The issue of “some college, no degree” hits across racial groups, but the disparities are higher among Black and Latino adults. More than 22 percent of Black adults and nearly 18 percent of Latino adults leave college without a degree, compared with about 16 percent of their white peers and only 9 percent of Asian adults.

**Figure 1**

If the entire population of adults who left college without a credential in 2019 received a degree, more than two-thirds (67 percent) of the population would be college-educated, translating to more than 30.3 million people. This achievement would also spill over by race, with more than 60 percent of Black adults and nearly half of Latino adults being college-educated. However, even if this scenario were to occur, disparities by race and gender would narrow but still exist. Black adults would trail white adults in attainment by 13 percentage points, and the Latino-white attainment gap would be 25 percentage points.

### Conclusion

Despite some attainment progress across groups, large and persistent equity gaps remain. As the Biden administration works to build a more college-educated population, any measures to improve attainment should be designed above all to improve equity, targeting race and gender gaps and reengaging students who left college without a degree. The federal government and states share responsibility for equitably raising attainment. As mentioned earlier, Congress and states should close funding gaps at [institutions serving](https://americanprogress.org/issues/education-postsecondary/reports/2020/10/07/491242/78-billion-community-college-funding-shortfall/)[larger proportions](https://americanprogress.org/issues/education-postsecondary/news/2020/12/08/492883/hispanic-serving-institutions-need-1-billion-federal-funding/) of students of color. Meanwhile, the U.S. Department of Education should explore options for conducting [equity](https://americanprogress.org/issues/education-postsecondary/news/2021/02/03/495334/biden-administration-can-now-make-college-affordable-accountable-racially-just/)[audits](https://americanprogress.org/issues/education-postsecondary/news/2019/04/03/465193/equity-audits-tool-campus-improvement/) to identify ways that colleges can improve outcomes for racially underrepresented students; and the administration should convene a commission of experts to identify the barriers contributing to student withdrawal and make its findings public.

[Nearly two-thirds](https://cew.georgetown.edu/cew-reports/recovery-job-growth-and-education-requirements-through-2020/) of jobs now require some form of postsecondary education, so a college degree is necessary to participate in today’s economy. Closing racial equity gaps would be an effective way to help meet the administration’s promise to “[Build Back Better](https://joebiden.com/build-back-better/),” especially in the wake of the pandemic.

# Degree & Credential Attainment

Ohio faces a workforce development imperative to address a widely reported mismatch between employer needs and job-seeker knowledge and skills. To successfully compete for business investment and jobs, Ohio must significantly increase the number of its citizens with postsecondary education credentials relevant in the workplace. For Ohio employers to prosper in a global economy, they must have world-class talent with verifiable knowledge and skills aligned with specific workplace needs. And for Ohio citizens to maximize their job, wage and career advancement opportunities, they must possess trusted credentials that reliably document their qualifications and readiness for employment.

That's why the Ohio Department of Higher Education established a bold [statewide goal for educational attainment](https://highered.ohio.gov/wps/portal/gov/odhe/initiatives/success-completion/degree-and-credential-attainment/attainment/attainment) in 2017: 65 percent of Ohioans, ages 25-64, will have a degree, certificate or other postsecondary workforce credential of value in the workplace by 2025.

Since establishing the attainment goal, Ohio’s overall rate of educational attainment has improved significantly, increasing nearly 15% in the past decade. To achieve this statewide goal, significant increases in educational attainment must occur for historically marginalized student populations: Blacks, Latinos, Native Americans, adults over the age of 25, and students from low-income families.

## Complete to Compete Ohio

Postsecondary attainment is critical to Ohio’s economy and our future as a state. As such, it is an important issue for more than just higher education. [Complete to Compete Ohio](https://www.completetocompeteohio.org/) is a public-private coalition of more than 40 member organizations from Ohio’s education and workforce systems, including employers, educators and the leaders of state agencies, statewide associations, unions, philanthropies and community organizations from across the state. The coalition’s mission is to raise awareness about the importance of earning the high-value credentials and postsecondary degrees that Ohioans need to earn a living wage and close Ohio’s skills gap, coordinate and collaborate on efforts to increase attainment and provide technical assistance to other champions of attainment.

For the past three years, the coalition has been hosting events to highlight the importance of attainment and its impact on individuals and on Ohio’s economy, creating communication tools, researching best practices and developing common points of advocacy. In 2020, Complete to Compete published [Bridging Ohio’s Workforce Gap: A Statewide Action Plan for Increasing Postsecondary Educational Attainment in Ohio](https://completetocompeteohio.org/wp-content/uploads/Bridging-Ohios-Workforce-Gap-Attainment-Plan-August-2020.pdf). This plan focuses on five key areas: Attainment Value, Workforce Alignment, Access and Affordability, Academic Success and Completion, and Regional Partnerships.

## Campus Completion Plans

click to expand

House Bill 59 called for each public college and university to submit a campus completion plan that was approved by their board of trustees to the Chancellor by June 30, 2014. The legislation further states that these plans are to be updated every two years. Completion plans provide a continuous improvement framework that can allow campuses to identify and implement strategies to increase the number and percentage of students earning meaningful postsecondary credentials.[Plans from each of Ohio’s public colleges and universities are available here.](https://highered.ohio.gov/wps/portal/gov/odhe/initiatives/success-completion/degree-and-credential-attainment/completion/campus-completion-plans)

## Scaling Up College Completion Efforts for Student Success (SUCCESS)

click to expand

In 2019, ODHE, the Ohio Association of Community Colleges, Stark State College and Owens Community College joined MDRC’s Scaling Up College Completion Efforts for Student Success (SUCCESS) project. Combining components from multiple evidence-support practices, SUCCESS is designed to improve graduation rates for traditionally underserved students in a financially sustainable way. SUCCESS helps states and IHEs align their resources with evidence-driven practices that move the needle on degree and credential attainment. For more information on SUCCESS, including its implementation in Ohio, [click here](https://www.mdrc.org/project/scaling-college-completion-efforts-student-success-success#overview).

## Initiatives Focused on Improving Higher Education Access and Success for Adult Learners

click to expand

One significant challenge to achieving Ohio’s attainment goal is that demographic projections estimate that Ohio will face a decline in the number of high school graduates in coming years. In order to bolster the number of Ohioans with a degree or credential, Ohio must increase the number of adult learners enrolled in higher education. Ohio has approximately 3 million adults between the ages of 25 and 64 who do not have a postsecondary credential. Of the nearly 470,000 students enrolled in Ohio’s public postsecondary institutions in 2017, close to 27% are adults over age 25. Since the Great Recession, the proportion of adult students enrolling in postsecondary education and training has been in decline; in the five-year period between AY2011 and 2016, adult enrollment has declined by nearly one-third. The Ohio Department of Higher Education (ODHE) is concerned by this enrollment trend among adult learners.

### Finish for Your Future

In 2020, as a response to these data, the [Finish for your Future](https://highered.ohio.gov/wps/portal/gov/odhe/initiatives/success-completion/degree-and-credential-attainment/finish-for-your-future/finish-for-your-future) initiative established the goal of increasing the proportion of adults over age 25 enrolled in public higher education from the current 27 percent to at least 40 percent by 2025.

Ohio is committed to providing affordable and equitable educational opportunities to adult students Additionally, Ohio will strive to close the equity gaps between underrepresented minorities and adults in enrollment and completion. Finish for Your Future has provided recommendations that build upon established initiatives and created a strategic framework of 24 recommendations to advance improvement of adult learner outcomes.

### Re-Engaging Adults in PostSecondary (REAPS)

Part of Ohio’s participation in the National Governor’s Association Educate 4 Opportunity program is focused on engaging adult learners. In 2021, the Re-Engaging Adults in PostSecondary (REAPS) working group was established to distill recommendations from Finish for Your Future, Complete to Compete, Strong Start to Finish, PLA with a Purpose and other agency initiatives focused on adult learners into a coherent set of policy recommendations that could serve to inform and policymakers seeking to positively impact the number of adult Ohioans earning a degree or credential.

### Competency-Based Education (CBE)

Traditional education has benefited millions of students – preparing them for college, jobs and careers – and it continues to do so. However, in recent years, there has been a growing trend of higher education institutions considering an alternative, competency-based education (CBE), to serve the needs of underserved adult learners. CBE is self-paced and personalized. It provides flexible schedules and pathways to meet individual needs. The time necessary to complete a CBE program can be reduced as it takes prior learning, prior knowledge and a mastery of competencies into consideration, rather than seat time or the number of hours spent in class.

In 2017, ODHE released a [report focusing on competency-based education (CBE)](https://highered.ohio.gov/static/files/uploads/board/condition-report/2016-Conditions-Report_FINAL.pdf) in Ohio which recommended the creation of an Ohio CBE Network of institutions interested in learning more about and/or developing and scaling CBE programs. Today the Ohio CBE Network with representatives from 26 Ohio public institutions of higher education serves as a forum for quarterly meetings and activities

The [Ohio CBE Network](https://highered.ohio.gov/wps/portal/gov/odhe/educators/academic-programs-policies/cbe/cbe) Steering Committee strives to create practical tools for colleges and universities interested in pursuing competency-based education to include a network of expert practitioners, and a repository of resources and best practices for CBE development, implementation, and sustainment.

## Initiatives Focused on Helping Students with Some Credit but No Degree (SCND) Complete their Education

click to expand

Approximately 1.3 million Ohioans have earned some college credit but have not earned a degree or credential(SCND). It is critical to the continued economic well-being of the State of Ohio that a substantial number of these former students earn a credential. Indeed, economists have indicated that increasing the number of Ohioans with postsecondary degrees or credentials is necessary for Ohio to remain economically competitive and meet the workforce needs of the future.

### College Comeback

In order to facilitate the return to higher education by Ohioans who stopped out prior to crossing the finish line, the Ohio Department of Higher Education (ODHE) has issued guidance for voluntary institutional debt relief programs titled [College Comeback](https://highered.ohio.gov/wps/portal/gov/odhe/initiatives/affordability/college-comeback/college-comeback).

### Second Chance Grant

The State of Ohio further strengthened its commitment to assisting students in attaining a degree or credential through the establishment of the [Second Chance Grant](https://highered.ohio.gov/wps/portal/gov/odhe/students/pay-for-college/ohio-grants-scholarships/second-chance-grant). The objectives of the Second Chance Grant are to reduce financial barriers preventing Ohioans with some college credit but no bachelor’s degree from returning to higher education and to increase the number of Ohioans with a degree or credential. The Second Chance Grant provides financial assistance in the form of $2,000 grants to eligible students re-enrolling at a qualifying institution in order to obtain a degree or credential.

# Degree & Credential Attainment

Ohio faces a workforce development imperative to address a widely reported mismatch between employer needs and job-seeker knowledge and skills. To successfully compete for business investment and jobs, Ohio must significantly increase the number of its citizens with postsecondary education credentials relevant in the workplace. For Ohio employers to prosper in a global economy, they must have world-class talent with verifiable knowledge and skills aligned with specific workplace needs. And for Ohio citizens to maximize their job, wage and career advancement opportunities, they must possess trusted credentials that reliably document their qualifications and readiness for employment.

That's why the Ohio Department of Higher Education established a bold [statewide goal for educational attainment](https://highered.ohio.gov/wps/portal/gov/odhe/initiatives/success-completion/degree-and-credential-attainment/attainment/attainment) in 2017: 65 percent of Ohioans, ages 25-64, will have a degree, certificate or other postsecondary workforce credential of value in the workplace by 2025.

Since establishing the attainment goal, Ohio’s overall rate of educational attainment has improved significantly, increasing nearly 15% in the past decade. To achieve this statewide goal, significant increases in educational attainment must occur for historically marginalized student populations: Blacks, Latinos, Native Americans, adults over the age of 25, and students from low-income families.

Expand All Sections

## Complete to Compete Ohio

Postsecondary attainment is critical to Ohio’s economy and our future as a state. As such, it is an important issue for more than just higher education. [Complete to Compete Ohio](https://www.completetocompeteohio.org/) is a public-private coalition of more than 40 member organizations from Ohio’s education and workforce systems, including employers, educators and the leaders of state agencies, statewide associations, unions, philanthropies and community organizations from across the state. The coalition’s mission is to raise awareness about the importance of earning the high-value credentials and postsecondary degrees that Ohioans need to earn a living wage and close Ohio’s skills gap, coordinate and collaborate on efforts to increase attainment and provide technical assistance to other champions of attainment.

For the past three years, the coalition has been hosting events to highlight the importance of attainment and its impact on individuals and on Ohio’s economy, creating communication tools, researching best practices and developing common points of advocacy. In 2020, Complete to Compete published [Bridging Ohio’s Workforce Gap: A Statewide Action Plan for Increasing Postsecondary Educational Attainment in Ohio](https://completetocompeteohio.org/wp-content/uploads/Bridging-Ohios-Workforce-Gap-Attainment-Plan-August-2020.pdf). This plan focuses on five key areas: Attainment Value, Workforce Alignment, Access and Affordability, Academic Success and Completion, and Regional Partnerships.

## Campus Completion Plans

click to expand

House Bill 59 called for each public college and university to submit a campus completion plan that was approved by their board of trustees to the Chancellor by June 30, 2014. The legislation further states that these plans are to be updated every two years. Completion plans provide a continuous improvement framework that can allow campuses to identify and implement strategies to increase the number and percentage of students earning meaningful postsecondary credentials.[Plans from each of Ohio’s public colleges and universities are available here.](https://highered.ohio.gov/wps/portal/gov/odhe/initiatives/success-completion/degree-and-credential-attainment/completion/campus-completion-plans)

## Scaling Up College Completion Efforts for Student Success (SUCCESS)

click to expand

In 2019, ODHE, the Ohio Association of Community Colleges, Stark State College and Owens Community College joined MDRC’s Scaling Up College Completion Efforts for Student Success (SUCCESS) project. Combining components from multiple evidence-support practices, SUCCESS is designed to improve graduation rates for traditionally underserved students in a financially sustainable way. SUCCESS helps states and IHEs align their resources with evidence-driven practices that move the needle on degree and credential attainment. For more information on SUCCESS, including its implementation in Ohio, [click here](https://www.mdrc.org/project/scaling-college-completion-efforts-student-success-success#overview).

## Initiatives Focused on Improving Higher Education Access and Success for Adult Learners

click to expand

One significant challenge to achieving Ohio’s attainment goal is that demographic projections estimate that Ohio will face a decline in the number of high school graduates in coming years. In order to bolster the number of Ohioans with a degree or credential, Ohio must increase the number of adult learners enrolled in higher education. Ohio has approximately 3 million adults between the ages of 25 and 64 who do not have a postsecondary credential. Of the nearly 470,000 students enrolled in Ohio’s public postsecondary institutions in 2017, close to 27% are adults over age 25. Since the Great Recession, the proportion of adult students enrolling in postsecondary education and training has been in decline; in the five-year period between AY2011 and 2016, adult enrollment has declined by nearly one-third. The Ohio Department of Higher Education (ODHE) is concerned by this enrollment trend among adult learners.

### Finish for Your Future

In 2020, as a response to these data, the [Finish for your Future](https://highered.ohio.gov/wps/portal/gov/odhe/initiatives/success-completion/degree-and-credential-attainment/finish-for-your-future/finish-for-your-future) initiative established the goal of increasing the proportion of adults over age 25 enrolled in public higher education from the current 27 percent to at least 40 percent by 2025.

Ohio is committed to providing affordable and equitable educational opportunities to adult students Additionally, Ohio will strive to close the equity gaps between underrepresented minorities and adults in enrollment and completion. Finish for Your Future has provided recommendations that build upon established initiatives and created a strategic framework of 24 recommendations to advance improvement of adult learner outcomes.

### Re-Engaging Adults in PostSecondary (REAPS)

Part of Ohio’s participation in the National Governor’s Association Educate 4 Opportunity program is focused on engaging adult learners. In 2021, the Re-Engaging Adults in PostSecondary (REAPS) working group was established to distill recommendations from Finish for Your Future, Complete to Compete, Strong Start to Finish, PLA with a Purpose and other agency initiatives focused on adult learners into a coherent set of policy recommendations that could serve to inform and policymakers seeking to positively impact the number of adult Ohioans earning a degree or credential.

### Competency-Based Education (CBE)

Traditional education has benefited millions of students – preparing them for college, jobs and careers – and it continues to do so. However, in recent years, there has been a growing trend of higher education institutions considering an alternative, competency-based education (CBE), to serve the needs of underserved adult learners. CBE is self-paced and personalized. It provides flexible schedules and pathways to meet individual needs. The time necessary to complete a CBE program can be reduced as it takes prior learning, prior knowledge and a mastery of competencies into consideration, rather than seat time or the number of hours spent in class.

In 2017, ODHE released a [report focusing on competency-based education (CBE)](https://highered.ohio.gov/static/files/uploads/board/condition-report/2016-Conditions-Report_FINAL.pdf) in Ohio which recommended the creation of an Ohio CBE Network of institutions interested in learning more about and/or developing and scaling CBE programs. Today the Ohio CBE Network with representatives from 26 Ohio public institutions of higher education serves as a forum for quarterly meetings and activities

The [Ohio CBE Network](https://highered.ohio.gov/wps/portal/gov/odhe/educators/academic-programs-policies/cbe/cbe) Steering Committee strives to create practical tools for colleges and universities interested in pursuing competency-based education to include a network of expert practitioners, and a repository of resources and best practices for CBE development, implementation, and sustainment.

## Initiatives Focused on Helping Students with Some Credit but No Degree (SCND) Complete their Education

click to expand

Approximately 1.3 million Ohioans have earned some college credit but have not earned a degree or credential(SCND). It is critical to the continued economic well-being of the State of Ohio that a substantial number of these former students earn a credential. Indeed, economists have indicated that increasing the number of Ohioans with postsecondary degrees or credentials is necessary for Ohio to remain economically competitive and meet the workforce needs of the future.

### College Comeback

In order to facilitate the return to higher education by Ohioans who stopped out prior to crossing the finish line, the Ohio Department of Higher Education (ODHE) has issued guidance for voluntary institutional debt relief programs titled [College Comeback](https://highered.ohio.gov/wps/portal/gov/odhe/initiatives/affordability/college-comeback/college-comeback).

### Second Chance Grant

The State of Ohio further strengthened its commitment to assisting students in attaining a degree or credential through the establishment of the [Second Chance Grant](https://highered.ohio.gov/wps/portal/gov/odhe/students/pay-for-college/ohio-grants-scholarships/second-chance-grant). The objectives of the Second Chance Grant are to reduce financial barriers preventing Ohioans with some college credit but no bachelor’s degree from returning to higher education and to increase the number of Ohioans with a degree or credential. The Second Chance Grant provides financial assistance in the form of $2,000 grants to eligible students re-enrolling at a qualifying institution in order to obtain a degree or credential.

# If Ohio wants to boost attainment, it needs to invest in career exploration



[Jessica Poiner](https://fordhaminstitute.org/about/fordham-staff/jessica-poiner)

8.11.2025

*   [](mailto:?subject=Have%20you%20seen%20this%20Fordham%20Institute%20article?%20&body=Have%20you%20seen%20this%20Fordham%20Institute%20resource?%20https://fordhaminstitute.org/ohio/commentary/if-ohio-wants-boost-attainment-it-needs-invest-career-exploration?)

![Image 3: attainment goal and career exploration blog image](https://fordhaminstitute.org/sites/default/files/styles/single_main_image/public/2025-08/attainment-goal-and-career-exploration-blog-image.jpg?itok=v9_koxTO)

Nearly a decade ago, state leaders [banded together](https://fordhaminstitute.org/ohio/commentary/governor-dewines-budget-shows-his-commitment-meeting-ohios-attainment-goal) to announce [Ohio Attainment Goal 2025](https://dam.assets.ohio.gov/image/upload/highered.ohio.gov/files/uploads/Link/Attainment-Joint-Statement-odhe_owt_ode.pdf), a statewide objective for 65 percent of adult Ohioans to have a degree, certificate, or other postsecondary credential of value by 2025. According to the [most recent state report](https://highered.ohio.gov/wps/wcm/connect/gov/dbe192ed-7008-47c7-8d1d-aed60d1b9bb0/Attainment-Report_2023_FINAL_070824.pdf?MOD=AJPERES&CONVERT_TO=url&CACHEID=ROOTWORKSPACE.Z18_JQGCH4S04P41206HNUKVF31000-dbe192ed-7008-47c7-8d1d-aed60d1b9bb0-p2n-Dth), we’ve made significant progress since then. Ohio’s overall statewide attainment rate of 52.3 percent is its highest since data collection efforts began. But it’s also nearly 13 percentage points short of the 2025 goal and 2 percentage points lower than the national average.

In the recently passed [state budget](https://www.lsc.ohio.gov/assets/legislation/136/hb96/en0/files/hb96-edu-comparison-document-as-enacted-136th-general-assembly.pdf), lawmakers called for a new attainment target to be set by December 31. As state officials debate where to set this new benchmark, they’ll need to consider how Ohio plans to meet it so we don’t fall short again. One source of [untapped potential](https://fordhaminstitute.org/ohio/commentary/ohios-untapped-potential-postsecondary-attainment) is Some College No Credential (SCNC) adults. Ohio, for example, has a [SCNC population](https://nscresearchcenter.org/some-college-no-credential/) of nearly 1.4 million. That’s more than the estimated 1.3 million adults who needed to earn credentials to meet the state’s initial 2025 goal.

Investing in and improving outreach and education programs aimed at helping these adults obtain credentials would be a great place to start. But addressing the root causes of _why_ so many Ohioans start but don’t finish postsecondary education is the only way to permanently fix the problem. [Academic readiness](https://www.edweek.org/teaching-learning/high-school-students-think-they-are-ready-for-college-but-they-arent/2024/02)—or, rather, the lack thereof—is likely the biggest contributing factor. Boosting student achievement, especially in [reading](https://fordhaminstitute.org/ohio/commentary/checking-ohios-early-literacy-reforms)[and math](https://fordhaminstitute.org/ohio/commentary/three-ways-state-leaders-can-address-ohios-math-crisis), will help improve attainment. But there are other contributing factors, too. And one of the easiest to address is how many Ohio students graduate without a well-thought-out plan for their next step after high school.

Each year, thousands of students graduate with [no idea how to pursue](https://www.the74million.org/article/74-interview-director-of-ohios-department-of-education-on-adding-workforce-to-name-and-mission/) their interests or even what they’re interested in. They know little, if anything, about careers or the job market. Many don’t realize that earning a postsecondary credential doesn’t have to mean a traditional four-year degree. Those enrolled at a college or university can take advantage of the career services offered by their institutions. But high school graduates who go straight into the workforce don’t have that option, and neither do the students who drop out and become SCNC adults. If Ohio did a better job of offering in-depth career exploration and guidance to students _before_ they graduate from high school, then tens of thousands of Ohioans would be better off.

To his credit, Governor DeWine has attempted to address the lack of career exploration and guidance available to Ohio’s secondary students. When he released his [budget recommendations](https://ohiohouse.gov/legislation/136/hb96) in February, he included a requirement for students’ graduation plans to identify career goals and align students’ high school experiences to those goals. This would have been a huge step forward. Unfortunately, the proposal [wasn’t included in the final budget](https://www.lsc.ohio.gov/assets/legislation/136/hb96/en0/files/hb96-edu-comparison-document-as-enacted-136th-general-assembly.pdf). An updated attainment goal did make the cut. But if policymakers actually want to meet that goal, they need to take career exploration in middle and high school seriously.

[Other states certainly are](https://www.forbes.com/sites/jeaneddy/2025/07/15/ensuring-all-middle-schoolers-are-well-positioned-for-future-success/). In Utah, college and career awareness is a [required middle school course](https://www.schools.utah.gov/cte/cca/?mid=3059&tid=2) for students in seventh or eighth grade and is taught by career-tech teachers, school counselors, and work-based learning coordinators. Idaho also [requires](https://cte.idaho.gov/educators-5/professional-development/middle-school-first-steps/) seventh and eighth grade students to complete one or more career exploration courses. Students in Washington have “high school and beyond” plans that are [informed](https://app.leg.wa.gov/wac/default.aspx?cite=180-51-220) by a career interest and skills inventory that’s administered by seventh grade and informs eighth grade course-taking. And in neighboring Kentucky, students develop an [Individual Learning Plan](https://www.education.ky.gov/educational/compschcouns/ILP/Documents/ILP%20Guidance%20Doc.pdf) within the first ninety days of sixth grade that [includes](https://www.education.ky.gov/educational/compschcouns/ILP/Pages/default.aspx) exploring careers and identifying which ones match their skills and interests.

The Kentucky Department of Education notes that its plans are “changing how students prepare themselves for their future.” To keep up with other states—and to do right by students and families—Ohio needs to change how its students prepare for the future, too. Lawmakers should revisit Governor DeWine’s proposal for incorporating career planning into students’ graduation plans. And to ensure those plans aren’t just box-checking exercises, lawmakers should also require a [career planning course](https://fordhaminstitute.org/ohio/commentary/heres-how-make-governor-dewines-proposed-career-planning-requirement-work-better) in middle school.

Like the old adage says, there’s more than one way to cook an egg. But if Ohio leaders actually want to meet the state’s attainment goal this time around, they should probably get cracking on career exploration.

# If Ohio wants to boost attainment, it needs to invest in career exploration



[Jessica Poiner](https://fordhaminstitute.org/about/fordham-staff/jessica-poiner)

8.11.2025

*   [](mailto:?subject=Have%20you%20seen%20this%20Fordham%20Institute%20article?%20&body=Have%20you%20seen%20this%20Fordham%20Institute%20resource?%20https://fordhaminstitute.org/ohio/commentary/if-ohio-wants-boost-attainment-it-needs-invest-career-exploration?)

![Image 3: attainment goal and career exploration blog image](https://fordhaminstitute.org/sites/default/files/styles/single_main_image/public/2025-08/attainment-goal-and-career-exploration-blog-image.jpg?itok=v9_koxTO)

Nearly a decade ago, state leaders [banded together](https://fordhaminstitute.org/ohio/commentary/governor-dewines-budget-shows-his-commitment-meeting-ohios-attainment-goal) to announce [Ohio Attainment Goal 2025](https://dam.assets.ohio.gov/image/upload/highered.ohio.gov/files/uploads/Link/Attainment-Joint-Statement-odhe_owt_ode.pdf), a statewide objective for 65 percent of adult Ohioans to have a degree, certificate, or other postsecondary credential of value by 2025. According to the [most recent state report](https://highered.ohio.gov/wps/wcm/connect/gov/dbe192ed-7008-47c7-8d1d-aed60d1b9bb0/Attainment-Report_2023_FINAL_070824.pdf?MOD=AJPERES&CONVERT_TO=url&CACHEID=ROOTWORKSPACE.Z18_JQGCH4S04P41206HNUKVF31000-dbe192ed-7008-47c7-8d1d-aed60d1b9bb0-p2n-Dth), we’ve made significant progress since then. Ohio’s overall statewide attainment rate of 52.3 percent is its highest since data collection efforts began. But it’s also nearly 13 percentage points short of the 2025 goal and 2 percentage points lower than the national average.

In the recently passed [state budget](https://www.lsc.ohio.gov/assets/legislation/136/hb96/en0/files/hb96-edu-comparison-document-as-enacted-136th-general-assembly.pdf), lawmakers called for a new attainment target to be set by December 31. As state officials debate where to set this new benchmark, they’ll need to consider how Ohio plans to meet it so we don’t fall short again. One source of [untapped potential](https://fordhaminstitute.org/ohio/commentary/ohios-untapped-potential-postsecondary-attainment) is Some College No Credential (SCNC) adults. Ohio, for example, has a [SCNC population](https://nscresearchcenter.org/some-college-no-credential/) of nearly 1.4 million. That’s more than the estimated 1.3 million adults who needed to earn credentials to meet the state’s initial 2025 goal.

Investing in and improving outreach and education programs aimed at helping these adults obtain credentials would be a great place to start. But addressing the root causes of _why_ so many Ohioans start but don’t finish postsecondary education is the only way to permanently fix the problem. [Academic readiness](https://www.edweek.org/teaching-learning/high-school-students-think-they-are-ready-for-college-but-they-arent/2024/02)—or, rather, the lack thereof—is likely the biggest contributing factor. Boosting student achievement, especially in [reading](https://fordhaminstitute.org/ohio/commentary/checking-ohios-early-literacy-reforms)[and math](https://fordhaminstitute.org/ohio/commentary/three-ways-state-leaders-can-address-ohios-math-crisis), will help improve attainment. But there are other contributing factors, too. And one of the easiest to address is how many Ohio students graduate without a well-thought-out plan for their next step after high school.

Each year, thousands of students graduate with [no idea how to pursue](https://www.the74million.org/article/74-interview-director-of-ohios-department-of-education-on-adding-workforce-to-name-and-mission/) their interests or even what they’re interested in. They know little, if anything, about careers or the job market. Many don’t realize that earning a postsecondary credential doesn’t have to mean a traditional four-year degree. Those enrolled at a college or university can take advantage of the career services offered by their institutions. But high school graduates who go straight into the workforce don’t have that option, and neither do the students who drop out and become SCNC adults. If Ohio did a better job of offering in-depth career exploration and guidance to students _before_ they graduate from high school, then tens of thousands of Ohioans would be better off.

To his credit, Governor DeWine has attempted to address the lack of career exploration and guidance available to Ohio’s secondary students. When he released his [budget recommendations](https://ohiohouse.gov/legislation/136/hb96) in February, he included a requirement for students’ graduation plans to identify career goals and align students’ high school experiences to those goals. This would have been a huge step forward. Unfortunately, the proposal [wasn’t included in the final budget](https://www.lsc.ohio.gov/assets/legislation/136/hb96/en0/files/hb96-edu-comparison-document-as-enacted-136th-general-assembly.pdf). An updated attainment goal did make the cut. But if policymakers actually want to meet that goal, they need to take career exploration in middle and high school seriously.

[Other states certainly are](https://www.forbes.com/sites/jeaneddy/2025/07/15/ensuring-all-middle-schoolers-are-well-positioned-for-future-success/). In Utah, college and career awareness is a [required middle school course](https://www.schools.utah.gov/cte/cca/?mid=3059&tid=2) for students in seventh or eighth grade and is taught by career-tech teachers, school counselors, and work-based learning coordinators. Idaho also [requires](https://cte.idaho.gov/educators-5/professional-development/middle-school-first-steps/) seventh and eighth grade students to complete one or more career exploration courses. Students in Washington have “high school and beyond” plans that are [informed](https://app.leg.wa.gov/wac/default.aspx?cite=180-51-220) by a career interest and skills inventory that’s administered by seventh grade and informs eighth grade course-taking. And in neighboring Kentucky, students develop an [Individual Learning Plan](https://www.education.ky.gov/educational/compschcouns/ILP/Documents/ILP%20Guidance%20Doc.pdf) within the first ninety days of sixth grade that [includes](https://www.education.ky.gov/educational/compschcouns/ILP/Pages/default.aspx) exploring careers and identifying which ones match their skills and interests.

The Kentucky Department of Education notes that its plans are “changing how students prepare themselves for their future.” To keep up with other states—and to do right by students and families—Ohio needs to change how its students prepare for the future, too. Lawmakers should revisit Governor DeWine’s proposal for incorporating career planning into students’ graduation plans. And to ensure those plans aren’t just box-checking exercises, lawmakers should also require a [career planning course](https://fordhaminstitute.org/ohio/commentary/heres-how-make-governor-dewines-proposed-career-planning-requirement-work-better) in middle school.

Like the old adage says, there’s more than one way to cook an egg. But if Ohio leaders actually want to meet the state’s attainment goal this time around, they should probably get cracking on career exploration.

Comple  tion

ABOUT THESE METRICS

While many states have made significant gains in postsecondary enrollment, rates of degree completion across the
nation remain below expected levels. The failure to complete a degree program has negative consequences for both
students and states. Since employers are more likely to demand an educational credential than a specific number of
postsecondary credits, a premature departure from college can severely curb one’s prospects for future employment
and earnings. For example, individuals who have attained a bachelor  ’s degree earn 14 to 26 percent more than those
who have completed 16 years of schooling without graduating from college.22 Similarly, individuals who have earned
a certificate or associate degree tend to earn significantly more than those who enrolled but did not graduate,
particularly in health-related and technical fields.23 In addition, when students fail to graduate, the state fails to
optimize its investment in higher education through lost institutional appropriations and student grant aid as well as
lost revenue from state income tax.24

Finance

ABOUT THESE METRICS

Substantial financial investments are required to create and sustain a P-20 educational system that meets state needs
for economic and social development. Altogether states allocated 10 percent of their budgets to higher education
in 2018,28 including general operating expenses (78 percent); research, agricultural extension, and medical education
(10 percent); and student financial aid (11 percent).29 Various factors influence funding for education within any
particular state, including the tax base and structure, enrollment, expenditures for other public services, and economic
conditions. Notably, state funding for higher education fell significantly following two major recessions (the tech
bust in the early 2000s and the Great Recession in 2007-2009), but the ensuing economic recoveries did not result
in reinvestment in higher education at pre-recession levels.30 States also differ in the strategies used to ensure that
postsecondary education remains affordable. Some concentrate funds into direct institutional appropriations, while
others may focus more on need-based student aid.

Comple  tion

ABOUT THESE METRICS

While many states have made significant gains in postsecondary enrollment, rates of degree completion across the
nation remain below expected levels. The failure to complete a degree program has negative consequences for both
students and states. Since employers are more likely to demand an educational credential than a specific number of
postsecondary credits, a premature departure from college can severely curb one’s prospects for future employment
and earnings. For example, individuals who have attained a bachelor  ’s degree earn 14 to 26 percent more than those
who have completed 16 years of schooling without graduating from college.22 Similarly, individuals who have earned
a certificate or associate degree tend to earn significantly more than those who enrolled but did not graduate,
particularly in health-related and technical fields.23 In addition, when students fail to graduate, the state fails to
optimize its investment in higher education through lost institutional appropriations and student grant aid as well as
lost revenue from state income tax.24

## Student  
Enrollment!Image 7: Student Enrollment - Photo of students in classroom setting

### Ohio Public School Students Ohio has 1.6 million public school students of varying backgrounds and characteristics.

![Image 8: Ohio student characteristics table](https://www.ohiobythenumbers.com/assets2026/img/2026-student-enrollment-01-ohio-public-school-student-charicteristics-table.svg)
**Source:** Ohio DEW, [Advanced Reports](https://reportcard.education.ohio.gov/ "Link opens in a new tab") (2024-25). **Note:** Public school enrollments include traditional district, public charter, and independent STEM school students, but do not include students attending joint-vocational districts and educational service centers, pupils attending non-public schools, or home schooled students. More information about those enrollments are found in the “School Options” section.

### Public School Enrollment by Grade Level Ohio has approximately 100,000 to 130,000 public school students per grade level.

![Image 9: Ohio students grade level table](https://www.ohiobythenumbers.com/assets2026/img/2026-student-enrollment-02-ohio-public-school-enrollment-by-grade-level-table.svg)
**Source:** Ohio DEW, [Advanced Reports](https://reportcard.education.ohio.gov/ "Link opens in a new tab") (2024-25). **Note:** To maintain consistency with historical data used to report trends on the following pages, this table excludes joint vocational districts. If they were included, the numbers of eleventh and twelfth graders would be 128,392 and 122,015, respectively.

### Public School Enrollment Trends Since 2009-10, overall public school enrollment has declined by 9 percent. White student enrollment has fallen by 23 percent, while African American student enrollment has declined by 2 percent.

**Source:** Ohio DEW, [Advanced Reports](https://reportcard.education.ohio.gov/ "Link opens in a new tab"). Pre-2020 enrollment data are not presently available in Advanced Reports, but were pulled from the database for prior editions of _Ohio Education by the Numbers._**Note:** The percentages refer to the percent change from 2010 to 2025. The chart displays the spring part of the school year, a convention often used in this guide.

### Public School Enrollment Trends The percentages refer to the percent change from 2010 to 2025. The chart displays the spring part of the school year, a convention often used in this guide.

**Source:** Ohio DEW, [Advanced Reports](https://reportcard.education.ohio.gov/ "Link opens in a new tab") (2009-10 to 2024-25). **Note:** The percentages refer to the percent changes from 2010 to 2025.

### Public School Enrollment Trends by Selected Characteristics Since 2009-10, English learner enrollment has more than doubled while the number of students with disabilities has slightly increased. The number of students identified as gifted has declined by 18 percent.

**Source:** Ohio DEW, [Advanced Reports](https://reportcard.education.ohio.gov/ "Link opens in a new tab") (2009-10 to 2024-25). **Note:** The percentages refer to the percent changes from 2010 to 2025.

### Children in Poverty In Ohio, about one in five children under eighteen are from families with incomes at or below the federal poverty level ($31,812 for a family of four in 2024). The percentage of children in poverty in Ohio is slightly higher than the national rate.

![Image 10: Ohio Students poverty and economic disadvantage chart](https://www.ohiobythenumbers.com/assets2026/img/2026-student-enrollment-06-ohio-low-income-students-chart.svg)
**Source:** Childhood poverty data are from the Annie E. Casey Foundation, [Kids Count Data Center](https://datacenter.aecf.org/data?location=OH#OH "Link opens in a new tab") and based on U.S. Census poverty estimates (data were not reported for 2020). **Notes:** Ohio reports “economically disadvantaged” rates but they are inaccurate due to changes in federal subsidized meals policy, and not presented in this report.

### Ohio School Districts and Typologies For analytic purposes, the Ohio Department of Education and Workforce categorizes districts into eight typologies based on their geographic and socio-economic characteristics. This publication displays various statistics by typology to illustrate patterns of enrollment and achievement across the state.

![Image 11: Ohio student school districts and typologies map](https://www.ohiobythenumbers.com/assets2026/img/2024-student-enrollment-07-ohio-school-districts-typologies-map-legend.svg)
**Source:** Ohio DEW, [School District Typology](https://education.ohio.gov/getattachment/Topics/Data/Frequently-Requested-Data/Typology-of-Ohio-School-Districts/2013-School-District-Typology.pdf.aspx "Link opens in a new tab"). **Note:** This map displays the border of each district and its corresponding typology.

### Public School Students by Typology 28 percent of Ohio students reside in urban areas, 35 percent are from suburban communities, 21 percent live in small towns, and 14 percent are from rural areas. Another 2 percent of students attend online charter schools.  
  
 The **Urban: Very High Poverty** typology consists of the Ohio Eight districts—Akron, Canton, Cincinnati, Cleveland, Columbus, Dayton, Toledo, and Youngstown—as well as the charter and STEM schools located in those cities.

![Image 12: Ohio students public school by typology table](https://www.ohiobythenumbers.com/assets2026/img/2026-student-enrollment-08-ohio-public-school-students-by-typology-table.svg)
**Source:** Calculations based on Ohio DEW [downloadable](https://reportcard.education.ohio.gov/download "Link opens in a new tab") files titled “District and Building Overview” (2024-25). **Note:** Public charter and STEM schools are assigned to the [typology](https://education.ohio.gov/Topics/Data/Report-Card-Resources/Supplemental-Information/Typology-of-Ohio-School-Districts "Link opens in a new tab") of the district in which the school is located. Online charters—also known as e-schools—are not included in a typology, since they can enroll students statewide. The charter and STEM school category consists of 339 charters and 8 STEMs.

### Change in Enrollment by District Typology, 2016 to 2025 Between 2015-16 and 2024-25, enrollment has declined across all district typologies, except for suburban, very low-poverty districts.

![Image 13: Ohio students change in enrollment 2016-2025 bar chart](https://www.ohiobythenumbers.com/assets2026/img/2026-student-enrollment-09-ohio-change-in-enrollment-2016-2025-chart.svg)
**Source:** Calculations based on Ohio DEW [downloadable](https://reportcard.education.ohio.gov/download "Link opens in a new tab") files titled “District and Building Overview” (2024-25) and enrollment calculations from Fordham’s first edition of _Ohio Education by the Numbers_ (2016). This chart uses 2015-16 as the baseline year based on data availability. The percentages in parentheses represent the change in enrollment between 2016 and 2025.

### Race/Ethnic Composition by District Typology A majority of students attending urban schools are African American or Hispanic, while rural and small town districts are predominately white.

![Image 14: Ohio students race/ethnic composition by district typology bar chart](https://www.ohiobythenumbers.com/assets2026/img/2026-student-enrollment-10-ohio-students-race-ethnic-composition-by-district-chart.svg?v2)
**Source:** Calculations based on Ohio DEW [downloadable](https://reportcard.education.ohio.gov/download "Link opens in a new tab") files titled “District and Building Disaggregated Race/Ethnicity” (2024-25). **Note:** For display purposes, the percentages for student groups representing less than 2 percent are omitted. API = Asian/Pacific Islander. Due to small numbers across all typologies, the American Indian/Alaskan Native student group is omitted from this chart.

### Selected Student Groups by District Typology Roughly 15 to 20 percent of students in the various typologies are students with disabilities; gifted students make up a noticeably higher proportion of students in suburban typologies than others; EL students make up a larger fraction of students attending urban schools.

![Image 15: Ohio students groups by district typology](https://www.ohiobythenumbers.com/assets2026/img/2026-student-enrollment-11-ohio-selected-student-groups-by-district-chart.svg?v2)
**Source:** Calculations based on Ohio DEW [downloadable](https://reportcard.education.ohio.gov/download "Link opens in a new tab") files titled “District and Building Disaggregated Disability/Gifted/English Learner” (2024-25).

### Ohio’s Twenty-Five Largest Districts by Enrollment (2024-25)

![Image 16: Ohio’s twenty-five largest school districts by enrollment 2023 - 2024](https://www.ohiobythenumbers.com/assets2026/img/2026-student-enrollment-12-ohio-public-school-25-largest-districts-by-enrollment-table.svg?v2b)
**Note:** Ohio Virtual Academy, a statewide e-school, is considered equivalent to a school district. This table does not include charter or STEM students as part of the district’s student population.

### Enrollment by Educational Model Roughly 80 percent of Ohio students attend traditional public school districts, while almost 120,000 students attend charter schools, nearly 180,000 students attend non-public schools, and 60,000 students participate in homeschooling.

![Image 18: Ohio School Options enrollment by educational model table](https://www.ohiobythenumbers.com/assets2026/img/2026-school-options-01-ohio-school-enrollment-by-education-model-table.svg)

### Public Charter Schools Ohio has 339 charter schools—also known as community schools—serving almost 120,000 students.

![Image 19: Ohio School Options public charter schools table](https://www.ohiobythenumbers.com/assets2026/img/2026-school-options-02a-ohio-public-charter-schools-table.svg)  
  
![Image 20: Ohio School Options public charter schools chart](https://www.ohiobythenumbers.com/assets2026/img/2026-school-options-02b-ohio-public-charter-schools-chart.svg)

Historical enrollment data were drawn from DEW, [Community School Annual Report: 2023-2024](https://education.ohio.gov/Topics/Community-Schools/Annual-Reports-on-Ohio-Community-Schools "Link opens in a new tab").

### Characteristics of Charter School Students Reflecting the location of charter schools in predominately urban areas, Ohio charter school students are disproportionately Black and Hispanic.

![Image 21: Ohio schools characteristics of charter students table](https://www.ohiobythenumbers.com/assets2026/img/2026-school-options-03-ohio-characteristics-of-charter-students-table.svg)
**Source:** Ohio DEW, [Advanced Reports](https://reportcard.education.ohio.gov/ "Link opens in a new tab") (2024-25), for demographic data. ### Interdistrict Open Enrollment Four in five Ohio districts participate in interdistrict open enrollment. Roughly 75,000 students open enroll, with participation—until very recently—increasing over time.

![Image 22: Ohio school options interdistrict open enrollment chart](https://www.ohiobythenumbers.com/assets2026/img/2026-school-options-04-ohio-interdistrict-open-enrollment-chart.svg)
**Source:** Enrollments are calculated based on school districts’ funding reports; see Ohio DEW, [Traditional School Districts Funding](https://education.ohio.gov/Topics/Finance-and-Funding/School-Payment-Reports/State-Funding-For-Schools/Traditional-School-Districts "Link opens in a new tab").

### Private School Scholarships More than 165,000 students use state-funded scholarships (often referred to as vouchers) to attend private schools. The large increase in participation starting in 2023-24 reflects expanded eligibility, as all students now qualify for some level of support under the income-based EdChoice scholarship.

![Image 23: Ohio school options scholarship program table](https://www.ohiobythenumbers.com/assets2026/img/2026-school-options-05a-ohio-private-scholarships-chart.svg)

Ohio DEW began reporting more detailed data in 2021-22, and numbers since then are from [Advanced Reports](https://reports.education.ohio.gov/report/nonpublic-data-state-scholarship-participants "Link opens in a new tab"). **Note:** The chart displays the total number of students in the various scholarship programs. For more information on each program, see Ohio DEW’s webpage, [Scholarships](https://education.ohio.gov/Topics/Other-Resources/Scholarships "Link opens in a new tab").

### Homeschooling More than 60,000 students participate in homeschooling; the number of homeschoolers significantly increased starting in 2020-21.

![Image 24: Ohio homeschooling chart](https://www.ohiobythenumbers.com/assets2026/img/2026-school-options-06-ohio-homeschooling-chart.svg)
